title: 38-10_Gr. of Packer
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
GRIEVANCE OF: )
) DOCKET NO. 22-43
JONATHAN PACKER )
FINDINGS OF FACT, OPINION, AND ORDER
Vermont State Employees’ Association (“VSEA”), on behalf of Jonathan Packer, grieves
the State’s actions in refusing to permit him to attend a virtual meeting of the Labor Management
Committee for the Vermont Psychiatric Care Hospital/Middlesex Therapeutic Community
Residence (“VPCH/MTCR”), a time when he was appointed to that committee by the VSEA as
its chair, and while he was on temporary relief from duty. VSEA alleges the State (“Employer”)
violated the CBA by denying its request to select its own representative to the committee.
VSEA has also included an unfair labor practice charge asserting the State violated 3
V.S.A. § 961 (1), when it interfered, restrained, or coerced Mr. Packer and VSEA in the exercise
of their rights guaranteed under 3 V.S.A. § 903.
The parties provided stipulated facts and presented briefing to the Board Panel comprised
of Robert Greemore, Chair, Alan Willard, and David Boulanger.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. At all times relevant to this grievance, Jonathan Packer, (hereinafter referred to as
“Grievant”), was a permanent status employee of the DMH, as an Associate Mental
Health Specialist.
2. The Respondent Vermont Department of Mental Health is an agency of the State of
Vermont with offices at 280 State Drive, NOB 2 North, Waterbury Vermont 05671.
10

3. At all times relevant to this grievance, the State and the VSEA have been parties to the
Non-Management Unit Collective Bargaining Agreements, ("the Contract"), in effect for
the period from July 1, 2020, to June 30, 2022. As such, the State, VSEA, and the
Grievant are entitled to all rights afforded to the employer, the bargaining agent and
employees by the Contract, the rules and regulations for personnel administration, and by
statute.
4.Article 1 of the NMU Contract provides in pertinent part that:
The State of Vermont recognizes the Vermont State Employees’ Association, Inc. as the
exclusive representative of the Vermont State employees in the Non-Management
Bargaining Unit.
5.Article 2 of the NMU contract provides in pertinent part that:
Subject to law, rules and regulations, including, for example, 3 VSA 311(a)(10) and 3
VSA 327(a), and subject to terms set forth in this Agreement, nothing in this Agreement
shall be construed to interfere with the right of the Employer to carry out the statutory
mandate and goals of the agency, to restrict the State in its reserved and retained lawful
and customary management rights, powers and prerogatives, including the right to utilize
personnel, methods and means in the most appropriate manner possible . . .
6.Article 3 of the NMU Contract provides in pertinent part that:
VSEA TIME OFF: Subject to the efficient conduct of State business, which shall prevail
in any instance of conflict, permission for reasonable time off during normal working
hours without loss of pay and without charge to accrued benefits shall not be
unreasonably withheld.
…
Subject to the foregoing, time off shall be granted in the following instances to:
….
(g)Members of Labor Management Committees for meetings scheduled by the State and
VSEA.
7. Article 7 of the NMU Contract provides in pertinent part:
…
3.The parties agree that Agencies, Departments, facilities, or local worksites may
establish labor-management committees. Upon written request of the VSEA or
11

the State, an Agency or Department must establish a labor-management
committee for a six (6) month period to meet periodically and to discuss a
mutually agreed upon agenda. After it is established it may be extended (or
reinstituted after it lapses) only by mutual written agreement for additional six (6)
month periods at the discretion of the Agency, Department and the VSEA. The
numbers of participants, selected in equal numbers by the appointing authorities
and VSEA, shall depend on the needs of the group and the agenda items to be
discussed and may exceed four (4) persons for labor or management with the
approval of the appointing authority in any instance. These Committees shall meet
as needed to discuss issues of mutual concern; provided, however, these sessions
are not for the purpose of discussing pending grievances or for collective
bargaining on any subject. In the event the parties call a meeting, the Human
Resources Department and the VSEA central office shall be notified at least three
(3)working days prior to the meeting and may participate.
8.Article 14 of the NMU contract provides in pertinent part that:
An appointing authority may relieve employees from duty temporarily with pay
for a period of up to thirty (30) workdays: (a) to permit the appointing authority to
investigate or make inquiries into charges and allegations made by or concerning
the employee; or (b) if in the judgment of the appointing authority the employee’s
continued presence at work during the period of investigation is detrimental to the
best interests of the State, the public, the ability of the office to perform its work
in the most efficient manner possible, or well being or morale of persons under
the State’s care. The period of temporary relief from duty may be extended by the
appointing authority, with the concurrence of the Commissioner of Human
Resources. Employees temporarily relieved from duty shall be notified in writing
within twenty-four (24) hours with specific reasons given as to the nature of the
investigation, charges and allegations. Notices of temporary relief from duty with
pay shall contain a reference to the right of the employee to request representation
by VSEA, or private counsel, in any interrogation connected with the
investigation or resulting hearing
9. At all times relevant herein, the Grievant has been appointed by the VSEA as a union
steward and as a representative and the VSEA chair of the Vermont Psychiatric Care
Hospital/Middlesex Therapeutic Community Residence (“VPCH /MTCR”) Labor
Management Committee.
10. In April and May of 2022, the other VSEA representatives on the Labor Management
Committee were John Berger (Associate Mental Health Specialist at VPCH) and Bridget
Aldridge (Nurse Supervisor at VPCH) and the management members were Stephanie
12

Shaw (Executive Director, Chief Nursing Executive at VPCH), Grace Winters (interim
appointment to Executive Director filling in for Stephanie Shaw at VPCH), Troy Parah
(Secure Residential Program Director at MTCR Facility) , Karen Barber (DMH General
Counsel, Waterbury), Daryl Hall (former VPCH CEO) and Tammie Ellison (DHR
Administrator, Barre).
11. On February 15, 2022, an incident occurred between Grievant and a VPCH patient which
gave rise to allegations of misconduct on the part of the Grievant.
12. On February 16, 2022, the Department sent the Grievant a letter, attached hereto as
Exhibit B, which placed him on temporary relief from duty (TRFD) with pay pending
investigation into the February 15 incident and stated in part as follows:
Do not engage in any work activity related to the Department of Mental Health
(“DMH”) without specific authorization of your supervisor. Unless specifically
approved by your supervisor, do not use any DMH equipment or access any DMH
files, including computer files. Do not visit your work site or other Agency or
DMH work sites, and do not contact DMH employees on work-related matters.
13. When State employees are placed on TRFD with pay pending review of an investigatory
matter involving alleged misconduct, the standard TRFD letter contains an instruction to
the employee being placed on TRFD that they not engage in “any work activity related to
the Department without specific authorization of [their] supervisor.” The State has been
using this language for over two decades. VSEA has been aware of the State’s
longstanding practice of restricting employees on TRFD from performing their job duties
on behalf of the employer, but VSEA has never waived its right to designate such
employees as its representatives and agents in its role as exclusive bargaining agent.
14. DHR Investigator Jim Morris was assigned to investigate the allegations against the
grievant and conducted the following interviews:
13

Person Interviewed, Witness/Subject Date of Interview(s)
Position
Michelle Uline Mental Witness March 11, 2022
health specialist
Renee Spaulding Mental Witness March 22, 2022
health specialist
Jessica Benway Witness March 21, 2022
Mental health specialist
Roger Hill Charge nurse Witness March 22, 2022
Samantha Lepage Witness March 22, 2022
Registered nurse
Jonathan Packer Mental Subject March 31, 2022
health specialist
15. On April 6, 2022, Investigator Morris forwarded an investigative report to DMH
Commissioner Emily Hawes and DHR General Counsel Thomas Waldman. In its last
paragraph, the report states that the Grievant was asked about the interaction with
Winters and Shaw when they placed him on leave, and that he admitted that he had been
sarcastic, and that he believed the employer’s actions were ridiculous and responded
accordingly. On April 15, 2022, HR Administrator Tammie Ellison scheduled a staffing
meeting on April 20 for the DMH Management team to meet with DHR Legal and DHR
Labor Relations staff to discuss the Packer investigation.
16. At some point in early April 2022, the VSEA and the Department scheduled a Labor
Management Committee meeting to be held on April 20.
17. On April 19, VSEA Field Representative Rachael Fields sent Human Resources
Administrator Tammie Ellison the message dated 4/19 at 1:27 p.m. which stated as
follows:
We have a LMC scheduled for tomorrow. Jo Packer will be attending virtually. I
have seen nothing in his investigation which warrants him not being present
virtually as a VSEA representative.
14

I have received the following agenda items:
1. MTCR staff feel left out when management sends email communications
which only mention VPCH.
2. A lot of the recruitment and retention issues may be related to hiring practices
and not supporting promotion within.
3. Training have become insufficient in that they haven’t been in person or via
Teams in years and often times are only emails. Please let me know if you
have more to add.
18. Ms. Ellison responded as follows on April 20 at 10:01 a.m.
After speaking with Labor Relations, the State contends that Jo’s participation as
a VSEA Steward at the VPCH LMC meeting today would be in violation of the
temporary relief of duty letter as the LMC is directly tied to his employment at
VPCH/DMH. Whereas if Jo was requesting to take leave to be able to attend a
counsel [sic] meeting, an executive meeting, training, etc. that would ne nor [sic]
a violation.
19. On May 4, 2022, a second staffing meeting was held between the DMH management
team, DHR Legal, and DHR Labor Relations to continue their inquiry into the allegations
against Mr. Packer.
20. On June 3, 2022, VPCH CEO Daryl Hall met with the grievant and discussed the
conditions under which he would return to work at the VPCH. Grievant was issued a
written reprimand, [Exhibit E]. CEO Hall advised grievant of two additional
expectations. First, Grievant was expected to successfully complete Pro-ACT training on
June 8, June 9, and June 10, 2023 and complete a written report detailing his
understanding of appropriate and acceptable de-escalation techniques to Grace Winters,
Interim Chief Nursing Executive. Grievant was also expected to complete four (4)
individual sessions with Dr. Greg Tomasulo, Director of Psychology, focusing on
awareness, non-verbal intimidation, and appropriate de-escalation techniques. Grievant’s
TRFD with pay status ended on June 8, 2022 and he returned to his regular duties after
15

completing the three days of Pro-ACT training. The VSEA has grieved the written
reprimand and the grievance remains pending at this time.
21. On August 1, 2022, the VSEA timely filed the instant Step IV grievance at the Labor
Board raising the challenges set forth in this grievance.
OPINION
The Union asserts the Employer violated the Contract, and the State Employees Labor
Relations Act (“SELRA”), 3 V.S.A. § 903, when Employer prohibited Grievant, its chosen chair,
access to and participation in a Labor Management Committee (“LMC”) meeting with
Employer. Although the VSEA has filed both a Grievance and unfair labor practice charge, the
Board must first review the Grievance to determine whether it is arbitrable or subject to the
dispute resolution process in the Contract. If it is, the Board must defer to that grievance
procedure. Parties to a collective bargaining agreement must first exhaust all contractual
remedies before an unfair labor practice charge will lie. See, e.g., Burlington Area Pub. Emps.
Union, Loc. 1343, AFSCME, AFL-CIO v. Champlain Water Dist., 156 Vt. 516, 518 (1991).
Grievant has alleged the Employer violated Articles I, III, and VII of the Contract. The
Contract provides a grievance process to redress noncompliance with the Contract. The Board
will defer to this process agreed to by the parties to resolve the present dispute.
The parties agree that Grievant was selected and appointed by the VSEA as a union
steward and as a representative and VSEA Chair of the Vermont Psychiatric Care
Hospital/Middlesex Therapeutic Community Residence (“VPCH/MTCR”) Labor Management
Committee. The Contract provides the Union with the right to appoint its representatives to
labor-management committees. Article 7.
16

The Employer asserts its actions did not prohibit Grievant from obtaining leave time for
VSEA activities, but “only restricted Grievant from entering the workplace and interacting with
patients and state employees.” Article 14 of the Contract authorizes the Employer to place
employees on leave pending the outcome of disciplinary investigations. Grievant was on
temporary relief from duty (“TRFD”) and instructed not to “engage in any work activity related
to the Department of Mental Health (“DMH”) without specific authorization of your supervisor.”
The TRFD letter contained language Employer has used for decades advising Grievant not to
engage in “any work activity related to the Department.” Grievant’s role at the Labor
Management Committee, Employer claims, qualifies as “work activity related to the Department
of Mental Health,” and therefore, it properly prevented Grievant from attending the LMC
meeting. The Employer contends enforcing the mandatory leave by preventing Grievant’s
attendance was consistent with its TRFD letter.
The LMC meeting was scheduled as a virtual meeting. Grievant would not be attending
in person. The subjects of the meeting were not related to Grievant’s conduct or his work duties,
but rather general issues of recruitment and retention, training, and communication. Grievant’s
role in attending the LMC meeting was to represent Union members and the interests of the
Union. Grievant’s attendance and participation at the Labor Relations Committee meeting was
not in performance of his job duties, nor on behalf of his employer.
The Employer claims that Article 3, Section 3, supports its decision to deny the request
for Grievant to attend the LMC meeting, The Contract provides “subject to the efficient conduct
of State business, which shall prevail in any instance of conflict,” requests by members of the
LMC for “reasonable time off during normal working hours without loss of pay and without
charge to accrued benefits shall not be unreasonably withheld.” Article 3. Because Grievant was
17

on leave and under investigation for alleged unprofessional behavior towards patients and his
supervisors, the Employer contends it properly denied approval for attendance at the LMC
meeting to avoid disruption of the work site and to promote the efficient conduct of State
business.
The LMC meeting was to be held remotely by ZOOM, not at the psychiatric hospital, and
none of the witnesses interviewed regarding Grievant’s alleged misconduct were to participate at
the LMC meeting. Compare Findings 10 with 14. The issues to be discussed did not relate to
Grievant’s job duties nor the subject of his Grievance. Grievant would also not be discussing or
using the meeting to litigate his grievance. Indeed, the Contract prohibits LMC meetings to be
used “for the purpose of discussing pending grievances or collective bargaining on any subject.”
Article 7, § 3. Grievant was not returning to his work site and would not be interfering with the
efficient conduct of State business to attend the virtual meeting.
The Employer relies on the response of Ms. Ellison to justify its denying Grievant his
right to attend the LCM conference. Ms. Ellison explains that although Grievant could attend a
council meeting, training, or executive meeting, he could not attend the LMC meeting without
violating the TRFD. The Employer has not sufficiently distinguished the duties of an employee
acting as a union representative at a council or executive meeting from that of an employee
acting as a union representative at an LMC meeting. The employee dons their union hat and acts
as a union representative when acting and participating in each of these functions. If attendance
at a council or executive meeting does not violate the TRFD letter, the Board is not convinced
that attendance at the LMC does.
The Employer has not presented any evidence that past practice supports its
interpretation that employees on TRFD are prohibited from participating in Union activities or
18

that Grievant’s alleged misconduct which precipitated the investigation and TRFD warranted
prohibiting Grievant from attending the meeting. The State’s history of using the TRFD letter
restricting employees from performing work related functions does not establish or demonstrate
its authority to prohibit those employees from acting as Union representatives nor deny such
representatives the ability to participate in LMC meetings.
The Employer denied the Union its right to have its chosen representative attend the
Labor Management Committee meeting, contrary to the clear requirements of the Contract.
19

ORDER
The Grievance of the VSEA is Sustained and the Employer must cease and desist from
restraining or interfering with the VSEA’s right to select its representatives for the Labor
Management Committee.
Dated this 23rd day of April 2025, at Montpelier, Vermont.

title: 38-1_Gr. of Wamsley
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
GRIEVANCE OF LEONA WAMSLEY ) Docket No. 22-38
FINDINGS OF FACT, OPINION,
AND BACK PAY ORDER
The issue before the Vermont Labor Relations Board (“Board”) is the back pay and other
benefits due Leona Wamsley (“Grievant”) as a result of her improper dismissal by the Vermont
Department of State’s Attorneys and Sheriffs (“Employer” “SAS”). On February 22, 2024, the
Vermont Labor Relations Board issued its Findings of Fact, Opinion, and Order, concluding that
Grievant was dismissed without just cause. 37 VLRB 189 (2024). The Board ordered the parties
to determine a back pay award and if they were unable to do so to notify the Board. A hearing
was held on May 30, 2024, on the back pay issue. On June 20, 2024, Employer filed its
Proposed Findings of Fact & Arguments regarding the Back Pay Award.
Findings of Fact
1. Grievant was terminated from her employment as a Secretary IV at the Chittenden
County State’s Attorney’s Office (“CCSAO”), within the Vermont Department of State’s
Attorneys and Sheriffs, effective June 8, 2022.
2. The Board Ordered Grievant reinstated on February 22, 2024.
3. Employer prepared a spreadsheet on which it listed Grievant’s gross wages due from her
termination until her reinstatement, reflecting Step increases, lump sum payments, and
other increases that would have been awarded to Grievant had she not been terminated.
Exhibit 1.
1

4. The second column of Exhibit 1 lists the biweekly entries for gross wages due.
Employer’s sum total for the second column of Exhibit 1, however, excludes the first two
rows of Grievant’s wages due.
5. Adding the total gross wages due column, including rows 1 and 2, to the remaining
entries for the gross wages due column in Exhibit 1, results in total gross wages due of
$85,206.70.
6. The total amount of gross wages due to Grievant is $85,206.70.
7. At the time of her termination Grievant was employed as a Secretary IV and had worked
for the SAS for over six years. She had received training and a certification as a
paralegal. Her job duties are further described in Finding #3 of our February 29, 2024,
Amended Findings of Fact, Opinion, and Order and incorporated herein.
8. After she was terminated from her employment, Grievant applied for unemployment
compensation through which she downloaded an app on her phone for job seekers. She
applied for paralegal jobs through the unemployment app and understood that her resume
was being sent to prospective employers.
9. Grievant did not seek a minimum wage job because she had a Paralegal degree, and
thought she could seek a position that used that training.
10. Employer challenged Grievant’s unemployment compensation award. Grievant did not
appeal the decision. Grievant mistakenly believed the denial would result in her not
receiving any benefits, rather than a ten-week delay.
11. Grievant enrolled in a Vermont Health and Human Services Program, Reach Up, which
assists people with children trying to re-enter the labor market with training and job
search and interview skills.
2

12. Grievant deleted the unemployment job search app once she registered and started
participating with the Reach Up program.
13. Participation in the Reach Up program required Grievant to work, intern, or attend
school. Grievant worked on her termination Grievance, which qualified as paralegal
work comparable to the internship she had at the CCSAO before she was hired as an
employee.
14. Grievant participated in Reach Up because she thought that was the best option available
to her.
15. Reach Up funds to Grievant were distributed through a card containing the sum of all her
benefits, including food stamps.
16. Grievant did not seek any employment opportunities or positions beyond Reach Up.
17. Grievant’s Reach Up payments included the $400 per month she had been receiving for
child support for her two minor children. The Office of Child Support received the child
support from the father of Grievant’s children and that amount was transferred to Reach
Up.
18. While receiving Reach up funds, however, Grievant did not receive child support.
19. Grievant participated in the Reach Up program from October 2022 until May 2024.
20. From October through December 2022, Grievant received $1633 from Reach Up. That
amount included $1000 from Grievant’s child support award.
21. Grievant received a total amount of $8820 from Reach Up in 2023. That amount included
$4800 from Grievant’s child support award.
3

22. Grievant was reinstated in February 2024. During the first two months of 2024, Grievant
received $1532 from Reach Up. That amount included two months of child support, or
$800.
23. The total amount of Reach Up Benefit Grievant received during her period of separation
from Employer was $11,985. Of that amount, $5800 was provided or transferred from
her child support award. Had she not participated in the Reach Up program, Grievant
would have obtained these funds as child support.
24. Excluding the funds Grievant would have received as her child support benefit, Grievant
received $6185 from Reach Up benefits alone.
25. Grievant was on Medicaid after her termination.
26. Although Grievant has been reinstated, Employer has chosen not to allow her to return to
work. Grievant’s status is paid not working.
27. Employer is contributing to her retirement, withholding taxes, and reenrolled Grievant in
the other benefits she received from Employer prior to termination. Employer has not
withdrawn funds from Grievant’s pay for Union participation.
28. Employer asserts Grievant’s back pay award should be reduced by the total amount of
funds she received through Reach Up payments and Food Stamps, $13,266.00, plus the
total amount of income she could have earned at a minimum wage job in Vermont.
29. Employer estimates that Grievant could have earned $33,173.60, had she worked at a
minimum wage job for eighty hours every two weeks. Employer’s estimate used a
minimum wage of $12.55 per hour and factored in a six-week grace period to allow
Grievant an opportunity to find a new position.
4

30. Employer asserts Grievant’s gross wages due should be reduced by a total of $46,439.60,
in mitigation wages.
31. Employer maintains Grievant could obtain a position earning at least minimum wage for
two reasons, her extended employment history and the low unemployment rate. Grievant
worked for six years and two months at the SAS.
32. Prior to working at the SAS as Director of Operations, Annie Noonan served as the
Commissioner of Labor for six years. From that experience, she has a general working
knowledge of the state’s labor market. During the period of Grievant’s termination, the
unemployment rate was low. In July 2022, it was 2.2%, in July 2023, 2 %, and in August
2023, 1.8%.
33. According to Director Noonan, the administrative support services field experienced a
small growth, about 1.5 % during the period Grievant was separated from employment
from the SAS.
34. Director Noonan did not know the hiring rates for individual employers or in the sectors
where Grievant may have applied. She did not research whether there were paralegal
positions available in the state during the period of Grievant’s separation from
employment. She was unaware whether there were any paralegal positions available in
Chittenden County or Vermont.
35. Director Noonan did not believe she could recommend Grievant for a position because
she had terminated Grievant for misconduct.
36. Grievant was terminated because Employer considered her behavior to be bullying.
37. Grievant believes that her reputation with her former Employer jeopardized her ability to
get another job.
5

38. Employer did not receive any reference checks for Grievant. Had the SAS received any
reference checks from prospective employers, it would have provided prospective
employers with Grievant’s period of employment. The reference check would not have
included a reason for Grievant’s departure.
39. Grievant was unaware of her duty to mitigate her damages. Employer did not notify
Grievant of her duty to mitigate damages.
40. Other than Reach Up or the Unemployment app, Grievant did not seek employment
elsewhere.
OPINION
The Board has authority to remedy the improper dismissal of Grievant. The Supreme
Court has limited that award to “reinstatement with back pay and other emoluments from the
date of the improper discharge less sums of money earned or that without excuse should have
been earned since that date.” Grievance of Brooks, 135 Vt. 563, 570 (1970). When calculating
the monetary compensation amount, the award should be limited to the amount necessary to
make the employee “whole.” Grievance of Goddard, 4 VLRB 189, 190-91 (1981). To make an
employee whole means to put the employee in the position they would have been in had they not
been improperly dismissed. See Grievance of Lilly, 23 VLRB 129, 137 (2000), aff’d, 173 Vt.
591, 593 (2002).
Employer argues Grievant’s back pay award should be reduced by the amount it claims
she could have earned working a minimum wage job for forty hours a week, and by the amount
of funds she received from the Reach Up program. An employee has a general duty to mitigate
damages by making reasonable efforts to find interim work. See Lilly, 23 VLRB at 137. The
employer has the burden of proving a claim of lack of mitigation. See id. To prevail in its claim
6

of failure to mitigate, Employer must show that suitable work existed and that the employee did
not make reasonable efforts to obtain it. See id. We have held that suitable work is new
employment which is substantially equivalent to the position lost and is suitable to a person of
Grievant’s background and experience. See Grievance of Lilly, 23 VLRB 129, 137 (2000), aff’d,
173 Vt. 591, 594 (2002). Grievant is not held to a high standard of diligence in seeking
employment and need only make a good faith effort to find suitable alternative employment. See
Grievance of Davidson, 29 VLRB 243, 252 (2007); Lilly, 23 VLRB at 137.
Employer has not proven that suitable work existed. Prior to her termination, Grievant
was employed as an Administrative Assistant IV at the Chittenden County State’s Attorney’s
Office (“CCSAO”). She had a paralegal certification and performed paralegal work at the
CCSAO. Although Employer provided general information about unemployment rates, it did not
research whether there were paralegal positions, or other positions substantially equivalent to the
one Grievant had prior to her termination. Employer presented no evidence to support that an
unidentified minimum wage job was substantially equivalent to the Administrative Assistant IV
position Grievant held at the CCSAO. Grievant’s back pay award will not be reduced by the
amount Employer claims she could have received from a minimum wage job.
Grievant made a good faith effort to find suitable employment. After Grievant was
terminated she filed for unemployment compensation. As part of that program, she downloaded
an app to find employment on which she uploaded her resume and searched for paralegal
positions. After Employer challenged her eligibility for unemployment benefits, Grievant
discontinued this process, not understanding that her disqualification would be temporary. She
thereafter signed up for Reach Up, which provided her with some remuneration and provided her
with assistance and accountability in researching education and training.
7

Grievant received a benefit or payment from Reach Up for participation in the program
which included the work involved in representing herself in her termination Grievance.
Grievant’s back pay award should be reduced by the amount she received in Reach Up benefits
alone, excluding the portion comprised of her child support benefit. The child support award
portion of her Reach Up benefit should not be applied to any reduction in Grievant’s back pay
award. These payments are not remuneration for work or training but represent Grievant’s pre-
existing award for the support and care of her children. The backpay award, therefore, should be
reduced by $6185, representing the amount solely attributable to Reach Up, which Grievant
received during her period of separation from SAS.
The total back pay amount of $85,206.70, less the Reach Up benefit awarded to Grievant
during her period of separation from the SAS of $6185, results in a back pay award of
$79,021.70. Grievant is entitled to interest on the loss of the use of this money through interest.
Interest is intended to compensate “the employee for the loss of the use of money represented by
the wages not paid the employee due to [her] dismissal.” Appeal of Davidson, 30 VLRB 363,
371 (2009) (citing Grievance of Warren, 10 VLRB 154, 155-56 (1987); Grievance of
Rosenberger, 29 VLRB 194, 204 (2007)). The award of interest is intended to offset the lost
opportunity cost of being denied wages or pay during the period Grievant was wrongfully
terminated and not working. The Board has added interest, at the legal rate, to a back pay award
to make an employee whole for income losses suffered as a result of an improper dismissal.
Grievance of Warren, 10 VLRB at 65-66. By awarding interest, the Board is not imposing a
penalty on management, but is simply compensating the employee for the loss of the use of the
money represented by the wages not paid the employee due to the dismissal. Id.
8

The statutory interest amount is twelve (12) percent per annum. The formula for
calculating simple interest on the back pay award is, Principal times Interest times time, or
$79,021.70 x .12 x 1.75 = 16,594.56
The interest is added to the back pay award to yield a total back pay award of $95,616.26.
ORDER
Based on the foregoing reasoning, it is Ordered:
Grievant shall be awarded the following back sum award of $95,616.26,
reflecting lost wages minus mitigation income of $79,021.70, and interest at a
12% annualized rate, in the amount of $16,594.56.
Dated this 29th day of January, 2025, at Montpelier, Vermont.

title: 38-21_Gr. of Draper
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
GRIEVANCE OF )
SHAWN DRAPER ) DOCKET NO. 23-16
FINDINGS OF FACT, OPINION, AND ORDER
Vermont State Employees’ Association (“VSEA” “Union”) filed a Grievance on behalf
of Shawn Draper (“Mr. Draper” “Grievant”) alleging the Vermont Department of Transportation
violated Article 47 of the Collective Bargaining Agreement between the parties when it denied
Grievant higher assignment pay (“HAP”) on days when he substituted for his supervisor.
The Vermont Labor Relations Board (“Board”) held a hearing on August 22, 2024,
before Board members, Robert Greemore, Chair, Karen Saudek1, and Roger Donegan. The
Grievant appeared and was represented by G. Alexander Robertson, Esq. The Department of
Transportation was represented by Assistant Attorney General William Reynolds. The parties
filed post hearing briefs on December 30, 2024.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. Grievant Shawn Draper is employed by the Agency of Transportation as a Senior
Operations Technician (“TSOT”) at the Dummerston garage.
2. Mr. Draper began working for AOT in 2001 as an Equipment Specialist. He has held the
TSOT position, previously called the Transportation Senior Maintenance Worker
position, since about 2014.
1 Board member Karen Saudek participated at the hearing, but did not participate in the
deliberations in this matter. See Section 11.15 Vermont Labor Relations Board Rules of Practice
(“The presence of two Board members constitutes a quorum with authority to conduct hearings
and to act.”).
21

3. The TSOT job classification is part of a series of job classifications referred to as the
Transportation Operations Technician (“TOT”) series, formerly the Transportation
Maintenance Worker series. These employees maintain the state roads including
clearing snow and litter and installing culverts and guardrails. The TSOTs are at the top
of the TOT hierarchy, below them are three TOT classifications I-III.
4. Grievant’s supervisor is Transportation Area Maintenance Supervisor (“TAMS”) II
Christopher Berg.
5. The TAMS is responsible for supervising the TOTS and TSOTs. The TAMS spends
time at the garage completing administrative duties. The TAMs also oversee work in the
field.
6. For off-hour operation issues, AOT contacts the TAMS first and if they are not available,
TAMS Berg forwards these calls to the TSOTs. Examples of incidents warranting these
off-hour calls are accidents, road closures, or animals hit on the roadway.
7. TSOT Draper has substituted for TAMS Berg in the latter’s absence. Grievant estimates
he has served in this capacity four or five times per year.
8. Before the fall of 2022, Grievant received higher assignment pay (“HAP”) when he
filled in or substituted for TAMS Berg. The difference in pay grade between Mr. Draper
and his supervisor was three pay grades.
9. On 8/5/21, AOT Operations Director Gammell and Deputy Director Law filed a Request
for Classification Review (“RFR”) for each of the four maintenance worker
classifications, including Grievant’s position, to accurately reflect the work and
responsibilities of these employees.
10. The RFR included a suggested four pay grade increase for Senor Maintenance Worker
22

classification from pay grade 20 to pay grade 24. The RFR outlined the following
responsibilities for the TSOT position “must provide all the duties of a TAMS in this
capacity without the supervisory title. In the absence of the TAMS (vacation, etc.) they
do perform the supervisory role.” Exhibit D.
11. Part of the impetus for the RFRs was to make AOT operation positions more
competitive and improve recruitment.
12. In drafting the RFRs Director Gammell and Deputy Director Law asked the District
Transportation Administrators, who were more familiar with the work performed by
their staff, to provide the first draft of the RFRs.
13. Many of the positions described duties and responsibilities that the workers had already
been performing for several years before the RFRs were filed. For years, the Senior
Maintenance Workers had been substituting for the area supervisor when the supervisor
was out. The Senior Maintenance Workers were the second in command.
14. The four positions for which RFRs were filed were the equivalent of the apprentice,
journeyman, master, and senior maintenance worker.
15. As part of the RFR process, AOT management distributed the RFR forms and draft job
specifications to the affected employees during a series of meetings called “tailgate
talks.”
16. On August 19, 2021, Grievant attended a “Tailgate Talk” at Dummerston Garage with
Shannon Gilberts, the acting General Manager for District 2. Gilbert brought the four
RFRs and job specifications to the meeting and left them for the employees to review.
23

17. Grievant was informed that his position and the other positions would be upgraded by
four pay grades. Grievant understood that the process was not completed and approvals
needed to be obtained.
18. Grievant recalled that “they put down the papers” for each of the positions, but did not
remember seeing the RFR documents.
19. Grievant signed a document acknowledging that he attended the Tailgate Talk, that the
different maintenance series RFRs were available for his review, and the duties of each
had been reviewed with him. “By signing below you are acknowledging that at this
Tailgate Talk on, 8-19-21, a supervisor or manager went over the class review RFRs for
the maintenance worker series.” Exhibit E.
20. The AOT Classification Committee (“Committee”) reviews RFRs. The Committee is
comprised of ten employees from AOT and the Department of Human Resources. On or
about September 21, 2021, the Committee met to review the RFR for the Transportation
Senior Maintenance Worker classification.
21. Initially, the Committee did not reach consensus on approving a pay grade increase to 24
because of questions about the level of knowledge, skill, and mental demand required
for the senior maintenance employees and requested additional information from
Director Gammell and Deputy Director Law.
22. Director Gammell and Deputy Director Law met with the Committee to answer
questions about the level of supervision and whether the Senior Maintenance Workers
would be expected to take on the higher-level duties of a supervisor in the absence of
their supervisor. Director Gammell and Deputy Director Law reported that the Senior
Maintenance Workers did fill in as acting supervisors and performed these higher level
24

duties.
23. The Committee requested that the class specification for the position be changed to
include: “[a]lso serves as a regular replacement for an AOT Maintenance Supervisor I
and/or II in their absence.” Satisfied with the change, the Committee agreed to upgrade
the pay grade for the position to 24.
24. On November 5, 2021, the Committee released a Notice of Classification Action to AOT
indicating the change in job title for the AOT Senior Maintenance Worker to
Transportation Senior Ops Tech and a change in pay grade from 20 to pay grade 24. The
effective date of the change was August 15, 2021.
25. It is not common for pay grades to increase by four points.
26. The pay upgrades were based in part on the need to recruit more people for maintenance
positions.
27. The Area Supervisor pay grade also went up three pay grades to a pay grade 27.
28. There was no input from AOT Human Resources or central office to change the
classification to include the requirement of serving as a regular replacement for an AOT
Maintenance Supervisor I and/or II in their absence.
29. In August 2021, negotiations began between VSEA and the State for the non-
management bargaining unit for the successor contract effective July 1, 2022-June 30,
2024. Gary Hoadley was the lead negotiator for VSEA, John Berard and Joe McNeil
were the lead negotiators for the State.
30. Deputy Director Law was not involved in the negotiations for the non-bargaining unit
taking place in the late summer and fall of 2021. He does not believe Director Gammel
was involved in the negotiation process.
25

31. The 2021 negotiations completed in October 2021, leading to an Agreement exchanged
on October 27, and executed on October 28, 2021.
32. The Union and State negotiated a collective bargaining agreement for non-management
unit effective July 1, 2022-June 30, 2024. Article 47 of the Non-Management
Bargaining Unit Contract addresses HAP and includes the following:
1. An employee who, in the absence of an incumbent, is assigned by the
appointing authority:
(a) To perform a majority of those duties of the higher level job which are
substantially different from his or her own duties; or,
(b) To assume the responsibilities of a higher level supervisory or managerial
job without any substantial change in duties; shall, commencing with the
third consecutive workday in which the employee actually worked a full shift,
be eligible for higher assignment pay, retroactive to the first day worked.
. . . .
7. Employees in the following categories shall not be eligible:
(a) positions designated as trainee classes
(b) automatic promotion classes
(c) employees whose class specifications clearly require them to fill in and
assume the higher level duties.
8. Employees assuming a supervisory position in an institution where the policy
requires such a person to be in a “charge” or command position, shall be eligible
for this differential for each full shift actually worked, and shall not be subject to
the three (3) consecutive days eligibility criteria in Section 1, above.
Gr. Ex. 1, at 63-64 (emphasis added).
33. Changes to Article 47 resulted in a reduction in the number of days needed to qualify for
Higher Assignment pay, from five to three. This Union gain was reached in exchange
for the Union agreeing to changes in the Commercial Driver’s License and emergency
closing articles.
34. The description of the ineligible positions in Section 7 of Article 47 did not change as a
result of the negotiations in 2021.
35. Grievant was assigned to perform duties of his supervisor TAMS Berg during his
26

absence from October 3, 2022, through October 15, 2022.
36. Grievant did not receive higher assignment pay while performing the duties of his
supervisor Berg from October 3, 2022, through October 15, 2022.
37. Grievant was assigned by AOT to perform the duties of his supervisor TAMS Berg
during his absence from November 21, 2022, through November 25, 2022.
38. Grievant did not receive higher assignment pay while performing the duties of Berg
from November 21, 2022, through November 25, 2022.
OPINION
Grievant claims the State violated Article 47 of the Collective Bargaining Agreement
(“CBA”) when it relied on the TSOT class specification to deny HAP to him. Grievant claims
the exception to HAP outlined in Section 7(c) of Article 47 does not apply to the circumstances
where an employee is substituting for their supervisor and otherwise eligible for HAP under
Section 1(b) of Article 47. Even if 7(c) applies to employees substituting for their employees,
the Union assets, it does not apply here because the reclassification did not result in a material
change because Senior Maintenance Workers, now TSOTs, substituted for their supervisors
before the reclassification. Finally, Grievant asserts the State should be estopped from applying
the HAP exclusion to Grievant and other TSOTs.
The State contends the Union has failed to sustain its burden of proving the State violated
the CBA, which is clear and unambiguous and excludes Grievant from HAP because his class
specification clearly requires him to fill in and assume the higher-level duties of his supervisor.
The Grievant has the burden of proving the Employer breached the CBA. When
interpreting the provisions of collective bargaining agreements in resolving grievances, the
Board follows the rules of contract construction developed by the Vermont Supreme Court. The
27

cardinal principle in the construction of any contract is to give effect to the true intention of the
parties. Grievance of Cronan, et al, 151 Vt. 576, 579 (1989). A contract must be construed, if
possible, to give effect to every part, and from the parts to form a harmonious whole. In re
Grievance of VSEA on Behalf of “Phase Down” Employees, 139 Vt. 63, 65 (1980). The contract
provisions must be viewed in their entirety and read together. In re Stacey, 138 Vt. 68, 72 (1980).
A contract will be interpreted by the common meaning of its words where the language is
clear. Id. at 71. If clear and unambiguous, the provisions of a contract must be given force and
effect and be taken in their plain, ordinary, and popular sense. Swett v. Vermont State Colleges,
141 Vt. 275, 277 (1982). If analysis of the contract language results in a determination that the
language is clear and unambiguous, extrinsic evidence should not be considered as it would alter
the understanding of the parties embodied in the language they chose to best express their intent.
Hackel v. Vermont State Colleges, 140 Vt. 446, 452 (1981). The Board will not read terms into a
contract unless they arise by necessary implication. In re Stacey, 138 Vt. at 71. The law will
presume that the parties meant, and intended to be bound by, the plain and express language of
their undertakings. Vermont State Colleges Fac. Fed'n, VFT, AFT, Loc. No. 3180, AFL-CIO v.
Vermont State Colleges, 141 Vt. 138, 144 (1982). The Board has a duty to construe contracts;
not to make or remake them for the parties or ignore their provisions. See Id.
Ambiguity exists where the disputed language will allow more than one reasonable
interpretation. In re Grievance of VSEA & Dargie, 179 Vt. 228, 234 (2005). The threshold
question of whether a contract is ambiguous is a question of law. Isbrandtsen v. North Branch
Corp., 150 Vt. 575, 577 (1988). In making this determination, we may consider evidence as to
the circumstances surrounding the making of the agreement as well as the object, nature and
subject matter of the writing. In re Spear, 2014 VT 57, ¶ 15, 196 Vt. 517.
28

The contract provision in dispute, Article 47, Section 7 (c), provides in pertinent part,
that “[e]mployees in the following categories shall not be eligible: . . . (c) employees whose class
specifications clearly require them to fill in and assume the higher level duties.” Article 47,
⁋7(c).The Union argues the language in Section 7(c),“is at least ambiguous as to whether it
extends to employees substituting for a supervisory position.” Union’s Brief at 14. The Union
asserts the term “duties” is ambiguous because Article 47 creates a distinction between “duties”
and assumption of supervisory “responsibilities.” The qualifying provision for HAP under 1 (b),
includes the term “responsibilities.” Section 1 (b) identifies employees eligible for higher
assignment pay, “who in the absence of an incumbent is assigned by the appointing authority: (b)
to assume the responsibilities of a higher level supervisory or managerial job without any
substantial change in duties . . . .” Because the limiting or disqualifying language in Section 7(c)
does not mention responsibilities, the Union argues, 7 (c) does not or cannot apply to the
employees qualifying for HAP under 1(b).
The plain and ordinary meaning of “duties” refers to “any action, task, etc., required by
or relating to one’s occupation or position.” Webster’s New World Dictionary of American
English (3d. Ed. 1988), at 42. The term “duties” in 7(c) of Article 47, does not exclude
supervisory responsibilities. On the contrary, the “duties” contained in 7(c) refers to those of the
“higher level supervisory or managerial job” to which they are assigned in the absence of the
incumbent. There is nothing ambiguous or confusing about this provision or the term “duties.”
The fact that the word “responsibilities” is included in the eligibility section, but not in the
exclusionary section does not render the latter section ambiguous. The exclusionary section
seeks to limit or exclude some of those employees otherwise qualifying under the broader section
of 1 (b). It is reasonable and not confusing that the language in 7(c) does not mirror, and is less
29

broad, than that found in 1(b). The term “duties” is not ambiguous or confusing and the Board
will apply Article 47, and the plain and ordinary meaning of its exclusionary Section 7(c).
Application of Section 7(c) to Grievant’s class specification demonstrates that he is not
entitled to HAP for the time he filled in for his supervisor in October and November 2022. The
class specification for Grievant’s position of Transportation Senor Operations Technician was
changed in 2021, to include the following: “also serves as a regular replacement for an AOT
Area Maintenance Supervisor I and/or II in their absence.” The class specification clearly
provides that Grievant should replace, fill-in, and perform the duties of his supervisor. Grievant
was not eligible for HAP when he filled in for his supervisor in October and November 2022.
The Union also relies on amendments made thirty years ago as supporting its claim the
parties intended that employees substituting for their supervisors should be eligible for HAP.
Neither the Union nor the State offered testimony that detailed or described the intent of the
parties at the time of drafting these earlier iterations. Moreover, the intent of the parties is best
determined by reviewing the words chosen in the applicable Collective Bargaining Agreement.
The Board has concluded the language of the applicable contract is clear and unambiguous and
the parties agreed to exclude from HAP those employees whose class specification clearly
required them to fill in and assume “the higher level duties.” Higher level duties include filling
in for a supervisor.
The Union also claims past practice does not support excluding HAP where employees
assume supervisor roles, because the State cites only one past practice. Where the language of
the contract is clear and unambiguous, the Board will apply its plain and ordinary terms and will
not resort to extrinsic evidence of bargaining history and past practice. See generally Grievance
30

of Vermont State Employees' Association (re: Annual Leave Accruals), 33 VLRB 330, 340
(2016).
The Union also asserts that the HAP exception should not apply here because the
classification change was a mere paper change to a job description without any connection to
classification review. The Union claims that “changes to a class specification should be
operative in denying HAP eligibility only if they materially informed a reclassification position.”
Union’s brief at 23. Although there is nothing in Article 47 that supports such a limitation, even
if the Board were to consider such an interpretation, the facts in the classification review for the
TSOT support application of the exclusion. The facts demonstrate that although the senior
maintenance workers had been substituting for their supervisors for years, to support the four
steps pay grade increase, the Classification Committee required the inclusion of language in the
specification that they “[a]lso serves as a regular replacement for an AOT Maintenance
Supervisor I and/or II in their absence.” Exhibit C. The inclusion of this language materially
informed the reclassification of Grievant’s position.
Finally, the Union claims that equitable estoppel should prevent the State from applying
the exclusion provision to Grievant and award him HAP pay. The use of equitable estoppel
against the government is rare and should only be used in extraordinary circumstances. See In re
Langlois/Novicki Variance Denial, 2017 VT 76, ¶ 27, 205 Vt. 340, 352. The party seeking
equitable estoppel against the government must establish all four of the elements of estoppel: (1)
the party to be estopped must know the facts; (2) the party being estopped must intend that their
conduct shall be acted upon; (3) the party asserting estoppel must be ignorant of the true facts;
and (4) the party asserting the estoppel must rely on the conduct of the party to be estopped to his
detriment. See Wesco, Inc. v. City of Montpelier, 169 Vt. 520, 524 (1999). Additionally, the
31

party seeking to estop the government must demonstrate that “the injustice that would ensue
from a failure to find an estoppel sufficiently outweighs any effect upon public interest or policy
that would result from estopping the government in a particular case.” In re Letourneau, 168 Vt.
539, 547 (1998) (quotations omitted).
The Union has failed to demonstrate the requisite elements of estoppel. There is no
evidence that the State bargaining representatives knew about the change to the TSOT class
specification that was recommended and approved by the Classification Committee. The State
did not have superior knowledge or withheld that knowledge from the Union. The State
representative John Berard testified that he learned of the reclassification of the maintenance
worker positions after bargaining had been concluded. This information did not inform the
contract negotiations between the State and VSEA. The State did not mislead or misrepresent
the status of that process or the results of that process. The Union cannot demonstrate that it was
ignorant of the true facts. The Union was aware that a potential reclassification was pending
during its negotiations.
Because the Union has not satisfied the elements of estoppel, the Board is not required
to balance the equities.
32

ORDER
Based on the foregoing findings of fact and for foregoing reasons, it is ordered that the
Grievance of Shawn Draper is DISMISSED.
Dated this 1st day of May 2025, at Montpelier, Vermont.
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
/s/ Robert Greemore
____________________________________
Robert Greemore, Chairperson
/s/ Roger P. Donegan
_____________________________________
Roger P. Donegan
33

title: 38-34_United Academics v. University of Vermont
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
GRIEVANCE OF )
UNITED ACADEMICS ) Docket No. 24-47
DECISION AND ORDER ON MOTION TO DISMISS
Introduction
The University of Vermont, (“UVM” “University”), has filed with the Vermont Labor
Relations Board (“Board”) a motion to dismiss the Grievance filed on behalf of United
Academics (“Grievant” “Union”) asserting the Board has no jurisdiction to hear the grievance
because Grievant has failed to allege an injury in fact.
On 12/20/24, United Academics filed a Grievance alleging the University violated Article
20.1 of the parties’ Full Time Collective Bargaining Agreement.
Article 20.1 (a) of the CBA addresses the provision of medical insurance and provides
that members seeking to waive insurance coverage, must demonstrate coverage is available to
them under a non-University plan, and “[i]f the faculty member waived coverage for one year,
the waiver will not automatically renew in the subsequent year.”
On October 28, 2024, the University emailed faculty and staff the following:
Starting this year, UVM is moving to an Active Open Enrollment process for
benefit elections, including medical insurance. This means all employees must
actively elect or waive coverage during Open Enrollment to receive benefits for
the upcoming year. While this may be a new practice for some, it ensures
everyone reviews and can select the benefits that best meet their evolving needs.
. . . .
If you do not make an election during Open Enrollment for any of these benefits,
you will not be enrolled for coverage for 2025.
Grievance and Opposition to Motion to Dismiss Exhibit 1 (emphasis in original).
34

DECISION
The University has filed a motion to dismiss asserting the Union failed to state any claim
upon which relief can be granted because there is no actual controversy between the parties, and
therefore, the board lacks jurisdiction. The University maintains the Union has failed to allege
that any faculty was injured in fact by the actual enrollment process, and therefore, it has failed
to allege an actual controversy between the parties.
The jurisdiction of the Board in grievance proceedings is limited by the requirement that
there be an "actual controversy" between the parties. Grievance of Doheny, 34 VLRB 244, 246
(2018) (citing In re Friel, 141 Vt. 505, 506 (1982)). “To satisfy the actual controversy
requirement, there must be an injury in fact to a protected legal interest or a threat of an injury in
fact.” Doheny, 34 VLRB at 246 (internal citations and quotations omitted). Where future harm
is at issue, the existence of an actual controversy turns on whether the employee is suffering the
threat of actual injury to a protected legal interest or is merely speculating about the impact of
some generalized grievance.” Grievance of Boocock, 150 Vt. 422, 424 (1988) (internal
quotations omitted); Grievance of Moriarty, 150 Vt. 160, 164 (1991).
The Union claims Article 20.1 of the CBA mandates that medical insurance for eligible
faculty “begins on the first day of employment” provided that the application is timely submitted
to human resources. Article 20.1. The Union asserts that the Article does not impose a
requirement for faculty to resubmit their application to maintain their health insurance. Instead, it
provides that “if a faculty member waives medical coverage the waiver will not automatically
renew in the subsequent year.” The University, the Union alleges, has altered the process
outlined in Article 20.1, and converted the status quo or default from coverage to waiver and
imposed the burden of renewal of coverage on the faculty member.
35

The University alleges because no member was harmed by its changes in the Fall 2024
open enrollment period, the Grievance is moot. It claims that the Union has failed to assert that
any member has suffered financial harm or been injured by the new policy. The University,
however, has notified faculty of the new policy “starting this year.” The language chosen by the
University suggests that the change will continue in the succeeding years. There remains a threat
of actual injury to a protected legal interest. That no member suffered the loss of their insurance
benefit this year does not minimize or eliminate the risk of such a gap in coverage the next open
enrollment period.
The Vermont Labor Relations Board seeks to resolve an issue on the merits, unless the
Board Rules of Practice or the Collective Bargaining Agreement require it to be dismissed on
procedural grounds. See Grievance of Adam Mickel, 33 VLRB 282, (2016) (citing Grievance of
Monti,10 VLRB 246 (1987)).
At this stage in the litigation, because there remains a future risk or threat of harm to unit
members, the Board will not dismiss the Grievance.
36

ORDER
For the reasons stated above, the motion to dismiss filed by the University is DENIED.
Dated this 23rd day of June 2025, at Montpelier, Vermont.
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
/s/ Robert Greemore
__________________________________
Robert Greemore, Chairperson
/s/ Alan Willard
___________________________________
Alan Willard
/s/ Roger Donegan

Roger Donegan
