title: 38-38_Vermont State Employees' Association v. Vermont Department of Human Resources and Department of Corrections
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
VERMONT STATE EMPLOYEES’
ASSOCIATION DOCKET NO. 22-39
v.
STATE OF VERMONT,
DEPARTMENT OF HUMAN
RESOURCES AND DEPARTMENT
OF CORRECTIONS
FINDINGS OF FACT, OPINION, AND ORDER
The Vermont State Employees’ Association, Inc. (“VSEA”) filed an unfair labor practice
charge alleging that the State violated 3 V.S.A. § 961(1) and (5) when it refused to bargain with
the VSEA and “bypassed the bargaining agent by communicating directly with VSEA unit
members and bargained in the press.” VSEA requests as a remedy that this Board order the State
to cease and desist, and to make whole any affected employees for their losses. The State filed a
response to the charge and a motion to dismiss. On October 8, 2024, the Vermont Labor
Relations Board issued an Unfair Labor Practice Complaint.
The parties provided stipulated facts and presented briefs to the Board Panel comprised
of David Boulanger, Acting Chair, Alan Willard, and Michelle Phelps.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Parties
1. The Vermont State Employees' Association, Inc. ("VSEA") is an employee organization
as that term is defined in 3 V.S.A. §902(6) with offices at 155 State Street, Montpelier,
Vermont 05602, and is the certified collective bargaining agent for the Supervisory and
Corrections Bargaining Units of the Executive Branch of the State of Vermont.
38

2. The State of Vermont is an employer herein as that term is defined in 3 V.S.A. §902(7)
and is represented for collective bargaining by the Department of Human Resources, with
a principal office at 120 State Street in Montpelier, Vermont 05620.
3. The employer herein is the State of Vermont and its Department of Corrections (“DOC”)
and Department of Human Resources (“DHR”) (collectively referred to as “the State”).
Facts relating to the Unfair Labor Practice Charge
4. At all times relevant herein, the VSEA and the State have been parties to collective
bargaining agreements for the Supervisory and Corrections Bargaining Units
(“Contracts”) in effect for the period from July 1, 2020 to June 30, 2022, and July 1, 2022
to June 30, 2024. See Exhibits A1, A2, B1, and B2.
5. The Contracts include articles titled “Management Rights” that include the following
provisions:
The parties will negotiate as required by law over any dispute arising under
paragraph 1, provided said condition of employment is a mandatory bargaining
subject. The parties shall meet within ten (10) days (unless mutually agreed to
extend) after a request for negotiations by either party and thereafter on a regular
basis. At the end of a forty-five (45) calendar day period, which shall commence
with the beginning of negotiations, the State may implement any proposed change
or new condition of employment, whether or not the parties will have bargained to
genuine impasse. The VSEA shall retain all statutory impasse procedure rights as
may be lawfully available to VSEA during the life of this Agreement except as
otherwise provided in the Employee Workweek/Work Location/Work Shift
Article. With respect to any dispute under paragraphs 2, 3, and 4, the parties agree
that they have fully bargained and any disputes thereunder will be processed
according to the grievance procedure.
See Exhibit A1, A2, B1, and B2, all at Article 2.5
6. The Contracts include articles titled “Employee Workweek/Work Location/Work Shift”
that include the following provisions:
2. NEW SHIFTS/WORKWEEK
In any department or institution, prior to establishment of a new shift (a shift with
starting and quitting time different from any existing shift) or a new workweek (a
39

combination of workdays constituting forty (40) hours (or eighty (80)) hours
biweekly if applicable) which is different from any existing combination of
workdays, or which includes evenings or half days, the State shall notify the
VSEA and will meet, if requested within ten (10) days, on a regular basis to
negotiate the impact of this decision for up to forty-five (45) calendar days. At the
end of the forty-five (45) calendar day period commencing from the date VSEA
requests negotiations the State may implement its proposed new shift or new
workweek without further negotiations or recourse to the statutory impasse
procedure.
See Exhibit A1, A2, B1, and B2, Article 20.2.
7. No shift or work week exceeding 40 hours in a week or 80 hours biweekly has been
created or established within the bargaining units without agreement of the Parties or
through the imposition of a contract by the VLRB.
8. DHR Labor Relations Director John Berard’s July 5, 2022 communication to VSEA’s
Executive Director Steve Howard and Director of Labor Relations Gary Hoadley
referenced at Paragraph 9 of the Charge is attached as Exhibit C.
9. Commissioner Deml’s July 6, 2022 communication to all DOC employees referenced at
Paragraph 10 of the Charge is attached as Exhibit D.
10. The State’s July 6, 2022 press release titled “Vermont DOC to Implement ‘Stability and
sustainability’ Plan referenced at Paragraph 11 of the Charge is attached as Exhibit E.
11. VSEA Director of Labor Relations Gary Hoadley’s message to DHR Director of Labor
Relations John Berard referenced in Paragraph 12 of the Charge is attached as Exhibit F.
12. The email communication between Mr. Berard and Mr. Hoadley transmitting Exhibits C
and F, herein, is attached as Exhibit G.
13. On July 28, 2022, the parties executed a side letter specifying certain temporary schedule
changes, recruitment and retention bonus and other monetary enhancements for
employees in the bargaining units. The parties met and discussed the contents of the side
letter in advance of executing the side letter. See Exhibit H.
40

14. On August 2, 2022, Mr. Berard rescinded his July 5, 2022, letter because “DOC no
longer intend[ed] to establish the new work shifts/schedules described therein.” See
Exhibit I.
15. To date, the State has not retracted its July 6, 2022 communication from Commissioner
Deml to all DOC employees. See Paragraph 10 of the Charge.
16. To date, the State maintains its July 6, 2022 press release titled “Vermont DOC to
Implement ‘Stability and Sustainability’ Plan” on its public website. See Paragraph 11 of
the Charge; see also: https://doc.vermont.gov/press-release/vermont-doc-implement-
stability-and-sustainability-plan.
OPINION
The Union asserts the State of Vermont Department of Corrections, (“State” “DOC”)
violated the State Employees Labor Relations Act (“SELRA”), 3 V.S.A § 961 (a)(1) and (5),
when DOC communicated directly with its represented employees on July 6, 2022, to the
exclusion of the Union, and communicated to the press regarding changes to the working
conditions before providing the Union any opportunity to negotiate a mandatory subject of
bargaining. The State responds that it did not decline or refuse to negotiate because it informed
the Union representative of the change in work hours, “absent a request to bargain” the impact of
that change. The State also claims the Commissioner’s email was not an attempt to deal directly
with employees or circumvent the Union, and that it did not denigrate or undercut the authority
of VSEA with its members. Finally, the State asserts that because the parties have successfully
bargained the shift change, the matter is moot and the Board lacks jurisdiction.
The charging party has the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that an
unfair labor practice occurred. See 3 V.S.A § 965(d); Castleton Education Association, Vermont-
41

NEA v. Castleton-Hubbardton Board of School Directors, 13 VLRB 60, 66 (1990). It is an unfair
labor practice for the State to interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in the exercise of their
bargaining rights. 3 V.S.A. § 961(1). It is an unfair labor practice for the State to refuse to
collectively bargain with designated representatives of employees. 3 V.S.A. § 961 (5). Working
conditions are mandatory subjects of bargaining under 3 V.S.A. § 904 (a)(3). Work schedules
which constitute working conditions are mandatory bargaining subjects of bargaining. VSEA v.
State of Vermont (re: Implementation of a “6-2” Schedule at VT. State Hospital), 5 VLRB 303,
13 (1982). Unilateral changes in mandatory subjects of bargaining “is the very antithesis of
bargaining and is a per se violation of the duty to bargain.” Essex Junction Education
Association v. Essex Junction Prudential Committee, 14 VLRB 107, 119 (1991).
Although the Board has not considered whether and under what circumstances direct
communication between management and members of a collective bargaining unit constitutes an
unfair labor practice, the Board has resolved the issue when applying the Municipal statute. The
Board has held that “school boards do not improperly circumvent the bargaining representative
and do not bargain in bad faith if direct communications with employees are non-coercive and
contain ‘no threat of reprisal or promise of benefit.’” Colchester Education Association v.
Colchester Board of Education, 19 VLRB 108, 11 (1996) (quoting Burlington Education Ass’n
v. Burlington Bd of School Commissioners, 7 VLRB 248, 250-51 (1984)(internal quotations
omitted)). The Board considers the totality of the Employer’s conduct in the context of when the
bargaining occurred to determine whether the Employer engaged in bad faith. See Rutland
School Board v. Rutland Education Association, 2 VLRB 245, 273, 276 (1979). An unfair labor
practice occurs when the employee reasonably believes that the employer was making a promise
42

of benefit, such as an attractive wage offer, or a threat of reprisal. Colchester Education
Association, 19 VLRB at 111.
In Colchester, we held that the invitation to teachers to participate in a committee
studying compensation is insufficient to rise to improper circumvention of the bargaining
representative and an unfair labor practice. The coercive impact on teachers was diminished
because the committee communicating with the teachers did not include any member of the
School Board with whom the teachers were negotiating. Id. at 112.
The Board found improper communications that contained a promise of benefit where the
Employer directly communicated to staff details about a report recommending proposed job
classifications, pay rates, and backpay wage assignments. See Essex Junction Education
Association v. Essex Junction Prudential Committee, 14 VLRB 107, 125 (1991). The details of
the report had not been presented to the Union as a wage proposal, although the employer
claimed the pay rates and backpay pay rates must be negotiated with the union. Id. Employees
“could reasonably conclude that the employer was making a promise of a benefit of an attractive
wage offer. The fact that the wage offer was not actually made to the Association caused
substantial damage to the progress of good faith negotiations.” Id.
The municipal standard for determining when an employer engages in an unfair labor
practice by directly communicating with employees, was developed in conjunction with the free
speech protection provision contained in the municipal statute. See Id. at 123. (citing 21 V.S.A.
§ 1728). The language of this provision is also contained in SELRA. “The expressing of any
views, argument or opinion, or the dissemination thereof, whether in written, printed, graphic,
oral or visual form, shall not constitute or be evidence of an unfair labor practice under this
chapter, if such expression contains no threat of reprisal or force or promise of benefit.” 3
43

V.S.A. §966. The Board concludes the standard developed under the municipal statute is
consistent with SELRA and will apply it to resolve this matter.
On June 6, 2025, Commissioner Deml communicated directly with the DOC labor force.
In his “WORKFORCE MESSAGE” he outlined a “DOC Stability and Sustainability Plan”
containing five goals that included a system-wide Vermont DOC 50/50 Work/life Balance 12-
hour shift schedule, including an extended three day weekend off per pay period, a market factor
analysis to study compensation, investment in professional development, staff wellness, and data
research and analysis. After outlining the five goals in detail the Commissioner concluded,
“[t]his is the plan. It will evolve and we will adapt. But, with this roadmap in place, we can begin
this work in earnest.” Exhibit D. Commissioner Deml did not send the email to the VSEA.
In his message, the Commissioner made representations about the VSEA and its inability
or failure to work in partnership with him. “I made a series of proposals to the Vermont State
Employees Association (VSEA) to accomplish this work in partnership, but we were not able to
reach an agreement.” After claiming the Union failed to respond to his plan, the Commissioner
turned directly to employees. “So now I turn to you with our plan of action.” Exhibit D. The
Commissioner also supported his plan by referencing a survey which he claims VSEA conducted
showing that “80% of [NECC] staff supported continuation of the new 12-hour shift model.” Id.
The stipulated facts do not support nor represent that VSEA conducted such a survey. VSEA
represents that it did not conduct this survey.
Although the Commissioner recognized that implementation would require partnership
with stakeholders, including VSEA and policymakers, he did not acknowledge nor notify
employees that such topics were required subjects of bargaining or required participation and
agreement of VSEA before the plan could commence. Adding VSEA to the group of other
44

stakeholders with whom DOC seeks partnership, does not adequately chronicle the requisite
level of engagement and bargaining with the Union required before the plan could be ratified or
implemented.
On the same day Commissioner Deml distributed his email, DOC issued a press release
announcing that it “will move from 8-hour to 12-hour shifts and the state will conduct a market
factor analysis of corrections security staff pay.” Exhibit E. The press release noted that the
change was definitive and going to happen. “The schedule change will take effect . . . on August
28, 2022.” Id. The press release promises the benefit of an increase in staff pay and new
recruitment incentives for staff bringing in new employees.
Employees reading Commissioner Deml’s email and the press release could reasonably
believe that the State was promising a benefit of “50/50 Work/Life Balance 12-hour Shift
Schedule,” “increases in security staff pay,” and “new recruitment referral incentives for staff.”
The State made promises of changes to the work schedule, an increase in pay, and other benefits.
The plan was developed and communicated directly to staff. The message leads an employee to
reasonably believe that all of these benefits will happen. VSEA, in contrast, appears ineffective
or unresponsive to management’s promised benefits for employees.
The Union has demonstrated by a preponderance of the evidence that the actions of DOC
in directly communicating with the members of the unit and the public violate the duty to bargain
and interfered with the employees’ exercise of their rights in violation of 21 V.S.A. §1726 (a)(1)
and (5).
Although perhaps well intended, DOC interfered with the relationship between the
exclusive bargaining agent and the DOC employees which constitutes an unfair labor practice.
45

Rather than negotiate directly with the Union about a mandatory subject of bargaining, the
Employer communicated directly with the membership.
The State argues there was no interference because the Union did not respond to
management’s request to negotiate the impact of the decision. Management, however, never
engaged in, nor broached the topic of bargaining the mandatory subject of whether and how to
change work hours. The work hour change management represented it would implement does
not qualify as a new “workweek” as that term is defined in Article 20, Section 2. The initial
stages of the plan called for a sixty hour work week- five 12 hour shifts and two days off.
Rather than a subject of impact bargaining under Article 20, the decision or plan to move to a
twelve hour shift was a mandatory subject of bargaining.
Mr. Berard’s June 5, 2022, email did not seek negotiation on whether changes should be
made to the shifts, but rather invited the Union to negotiate the impact of the unilateral decision
management had already made. The State could not make these changes absent agreement from
the Union. The changes themselves required negotiation. Management was required to bargain
whether to change work hours, not leapfrog over this requirement to the impact of that decision.
One day after the email asking whether the Union wanted to negotiate the impacts of this change,
the Commissioner notified staff of these changes, and DOC issued a press release announcing
these changes and the date these changes would go into effect.
Management failed to engage in bargaining on the subject of whether and how to make
changes to working conditions, specifically work hours before the Commissioner communicated
his plan that the Department of Corrections “will move from 8-hour shifts to 12-hour shifts and
the State will conduct a market factor analysis of corrections security staff pay.” Exhibit D.
46

The day after Mr. Berard sent his notice to Union representatives, the Union responded
identifying the State’s misapplication of Article 20, and demanded to fully negotiate the
proposed modification to its represented employees’ work schedules, a mandatory term. Mr.
Barard immediately responded to the Union’s demand to negotiate the change in work schedule
by providing his availability to meet as soon as the following week. Exhibit I. Subsequently,
Mr. Berard retracted his July 5 communication requesting to impact bargain through Article 20
as the parties reached a side-letter pertaining to the mid-term contract modification “specifying
certain temporary schedule changes, recruitment and retention bonus and other monetary
enhancements for employees” at DOC. Exhibits H and I.
The Union claims the press release also evinces bad faith. The duty of good faith
requires “an open mind and a sincere desire to reach an agreement” and “a serious intent to
adjust difference and to reach an acceptable common ground.” See Chittenden South Education
Association, Hinesburg Unit v. Hinesburg School District and Hinesburg School Board, 8
VLRB, 219, 236 (1985), aff’d, 147 Vt. 286 (1986) (internal quotations and citations omitted).
The Board must consider the totality of the circumstances to determine whether bad faith exists.
The distribution of a plan including the date on which it would start, coupled with the false
statements about the Union and its alleged failure to respond to management offers and
initiatives, and the misstatements about a survey conducted by VSEA demonstrates bad faith.
The declarations made by DOC about its plan and the absence of any recognition or
acknowledgement that the matter was subject to mandatory bargaining with the Union does not
display the requisite serious intent to adjust the plan based on any difference with the Union or to
reach common ground. Instead, management declared “this is the plan” and when it would be
implemented.
47

Although the parties were able to reach an agreement, that does not cure nor negate the
underlying interference and failure to negotiate about a mandatory subject of bargaining. The
Employer did engage in this conduct which constitutes an unfair labor practice. The charge is
not moot because the underlying dispute that constitutes the charge is not whether to impose a
twelve hour shift, but rather whether the employer bypassed the VSEA to directly communicate
promises of benefits to the unit members and refusing to bargain with VSEA. The State does not
yet concede that it was required to negotiate with the Union representative about the subject first,
before discussing its impacts or notifying the unit members of the plan. This dispute remains
and is capable of repetition yet evading review and therefore not moot. See generally,
Burlington Firefighters Ass’n v. City of Burlington, 4 VLRB, 379, 384-85 (1981) (declining to
dismiss an unfair labor practice charge as moot where union alleged unilateral adoption of rules
and regulations of management during negotiations was refusal to bargain in good faith, despite
resolution of negotiations dispute), cited in, VSEA v. Judiciary, 35 VLRB 419, 424 (2020).
48

ORDER
Based on the foregoing findings of fact and for the foregoing reasons, it is hereby
ORDERED that the Vermont Department of Corrections Cease and Desist from communicating
directly with employees represented by the Vermont State Employees’ Association on or
regarding work hours or other mandatory subjects of bargaining.

title: 38-50_Grievance of VSEA-Tetreault
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
GRIEVANCE OF )
VERMONT STATE EMPLOYEES’ ) Docket No. 24-39
ASSOCIATION )
DAWN TETRAULT )
DECISION AND ORDER ON MOTION TO DISMISS
Introduction
The Department of Vermont Health Access, (“Employer” “State”) has filed with the
Vermont Labor Relations Board (“Board”) a motion to dismiss the Grievance of Dawn Tetreault
(“Grievant”) filed by the Vermont State Employees’ Association (“VSEA”), because Grievant
failed to timely file her initial grievance of her demotion.
On 10/7/24, VSEA filed a grievance alleging that the State violated the Non-Management
Collective Bargaining Agreement (“CBA”) by demoting Grievant without just cause.
For purposes of the motion to dismiss, Grievant has affirmed the following facts
contained in the Employer’s motion to dismiss:
Grievant received notice of termination on December 14, 2023. On that date, Grievant
received a letter, dated December 13, 2023, notifying her of her disciplinary demotion.
The VSEA filed a grievance contesting the demotion on January 11, 2024. The grievance
was filed with Grievant’s department head, rather than her immediate supervisor.
50

Article 15(3)(a)(2) of the CBA governs the Grievance filing period at Step II, and
provides the following:
(2) An employee may opt to bypass the Step I process and file his/her complaint
directly to the Step II (departmental) level. If bypassing Step I, an employee must
file a written grievance, in accordance with Section 2(c), above, to the head of the
employee’s department, within fifteen (15) workdays of the date upon which the
employee could have reasonably been aware of the occurrence of the matter which
gave rise to the complaint. (emphasis added)
DECISION
The Vermont Labor Relations Board seeks to resolve an issue on the merits, unless the
Board Rules of Practice or the Collective Bargaining Agreement require it to be dismissed on
procedural grounds. See Grievance of Adam Mickel, 33 VLRB 282, (2016) (citing Grievance of
Monti, 10 VLRB 246 (1987)). Where the collective bargaining agreement between the parties
sets out specific times for filing grievances at earlier steps in the grievance process, or before the
Board, and the grievance did not adhere to the timelines outlined in the CBA, the Board has
refused to consider the Grievance. See Grievance of Benoit, 31 VLRB 237, 249-50 (2011);
Grievance of Ulrich, 12 VLRB 230, 239 (1989), aff’d, 157 Vt. 290 (1981). The CBA provides a
means to resolve conflicts early in the process. See Grievance of Mason, 16 VLRB 222, 237
(1993). See also In re Bushey, 142 Vt. 290, 294 (1982). Failure to adhere to these timelines
impedes this goal of early resolution. See Mason 16 VLRB at 237.
Article 15, Section 3 of the CBA states that a grievance must be filed “within fifteen (15)
workdays of the date upon which the employee could have reasonably been aware of the
occurrence of the matter which gave rise to the complaint.” The Grievant received notice of her
demotion on December 14, 2023. The Grievance was filed on January 11, 2024. Although the
grievance was filed more than fifteen days after she received notice of her demotion, Grievant
51

argues that the grievance period did not begin to run until she started working in her demoted
position. Grievant argues the operative word in Section 3 is “occurrence,” and the occurrence is
the demotion and that did not occur until December 19, 2023. Filing the grievance on January
11, 2024, she argues, was timely filed within the 15 day deadline to file a grievance.
The language in the contract is clear and unambiguous and the Board will apply its plain
and ordinary terms. See Swett v. Vermont State Colleges, 141 Vt. 275, 277 (1982). Although the
demotion might be the occurrence, the grievance period begins to run when Grievant “could
have reasonably been aware of the” demotion which gave rise to the complaint. This is an
objective standard. The Board must consider when Grievant could reasonably have been aware
of her demotion. The Grievant argues that the date she started her new position was the date
when Grievant could have reasonably become aware of the occurrence of the matter which gave
rise to the complaint. That the first day of the demotion was not until December 19, 2023, does
not extend the date when Grievant could reasonably have become aware of that event.
Grievant was notified that she was being demoted on December 14, 2023. On that date,
she received a letter outlining the demotion and when it would commence. The demotion was the
matter giving rise to the complaint. December 14, 2023, was the date Grievant was notified that
she would be demoted and the date when she “could have reasonably become aware of” her
demotion. The time for filing a grievance was fifteen days from December 14, 2023.
Grievant did not file her initial complaint within 15 workdays as required under the CBA.
The Board will apply the terms to which the parties have agreed and will not alter the deadline.
52

ORDER
For the reasons stated above, the Motion to Dismiss is GRANTED.
Dated this 30th day of June 2025, at Montpelier, Vermont.

title: 38-54_Grievance of United Academics
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
GRIEVANCE OF )
UNITED ACADEMICS ) Docket No. 25-05
DECISION AND ORDER ON MOTION TO DISMISS
Introduction
On 1/16/25, United Academics (“Union”) filed a Grievance with the Vermont Labor
Relations Board (“Board”) alleging the University of Vermont, (“UVM” “University”), violated
Articles 16.1 and 16.2 of the of the parties’ Collective Bargaining Agreement (“CBA”) and past
practice associated with these articles when it unilaterally imposed the “Course Equivalencies
Guidelines” (“Guidelines”) on the College of Education and Social Services. Articles 16.1 and
16.2 of the CBA govern faculty workloads. Article 16.1 contains the following provision.
“Unless the faculty member is told otherwise by July 1 for 12 month faculty and by June 1 for all
other faculty, the workload plan developed by the faculty member and Chair for the Submission
to the Dean shall be considered approved by the Dean.”
The University has filed with the Board a motion to dismiss asserting the Union failed to
file a timely Grievance with the University because it was filed more than thirty days after the
challenged Guidelines went into effect, and the Union failed to allege an injury to a member and
the Board lacks jurisdiction to hear the Grievance.
Background
The CBA outlines the process for distributing approved course equivalency guidelines.
“Upon approval by the Dean and Provost, these course equivalency guidelines shall be
distributed to faculty and posted electronically, and also sent to the Union, and will be
implemented in the immediately subsequent academic year.” Article 16.15. The Office of the
54

Provost approved the Guidelines on March 22, 2022, and they were posted online and distributed
to the Union.
The Union filed its Grievance with the University on October 8, 2024.
DECISION
The Employer has filed a motion to dismiss claiming the grievance was not timely filed
with UVM and the Union failed to allege an actual harm or injury, and therefore, the Board lacks
jurisdiction to hear the grievance.
The Vermont Labor Relations Board seeks to resolve an issue on the merits, unless the
Board Rules of Practice or the Collective Bargaining Agreement require it to be dismissed on
procedural grounds. See Grievance of Adam Mickel, 33 VLRB 282, (2016) (citing Grievance of
Monti, 10 VLRB 246 (1987)). Where the collective bargaining agreement between the parties
sets out specific times for filing grievances at earlier steps in the grievance process, or before the
Board, and the grievance did not adhere to the timelines outlined in the CBA, the Board has
refused to consider the Grievance. See Grievance of Benoit, 31 VLRB 237, 249-50 (2011);
Grievance of Ulrich, 12 VLRB 230, 239 (1989), aff’d, 157 Vt. 290 (1981). The CBA provides a
means to resolve conflicts early in the process. See Grievance of Mason, 16 VLRB 222, 237
(1993). See also In re Bushey, 142 Vt. 290, 294 (1982). Failure to adhere to these timelines
impedes this goal of early resolution. See Mason 16 VLRB at 237.
Article 12.8 of the CBA states that “a formal grievance must be filed at the appropriate
step within thirty (30) days following the time at which the faculty member and/or the Union
were or reasonably should have been aware of the existence of the situation that is the basis for
the grievance.” The Union filed the Grievance with UVM on October 8, 2024. The Union
alleges the Guidelines impose the condition that workloads can be changed up to the Add/Drop
55

period. The Union claims the Guidelines violate the CBA and past practice because it extends
beyond July 1 the determination of the workload plan. The Union asserts the Guidelines negate
the predictability of the protections of Articles 16.1 and 2 and allow the University unfettered
authority to reduce faculty members’ FTE after the Add/Drop period, long after the July 1
deadline imposed by the CBA. The risk of reducing the FTE, the Union claims, can potentially
impact the financial and benefit status of faculty members.
The Guidelines were issued on March 22, 2022. The Guidelines provide the following:
CHAIR DISCRETION: The guidelines below are meant to aid chairs from all
departments in determining equivalencies for large classes. Final determinations will be
specified through the workload process.
. . . .
*Note that all courses are assigned a 1 Course equivalency on the workload and then if
the course is overenrolled, the instructor receives and additional “banked” credit to be
used within two years. The only exception is courses that are traditionally overenrolled,
or have been overenrolled within the last two years. If the aforementioned courses do not
meet the enrollment numbers required to meet the credit articulated in the workload, then
the workload shall be revised to reflect the actual course equivalency.
1. A 0.25-Course equivalency credit will be provided in the workload for 3-credit courses
with enrollments of 31-50 at the completion of the Add/Drop period.
2. A 0.5-Course equivalency credit will be provided in the workload for 3-credit courses
with enrollments of 51-74 at the completion of the Add/Drop period. Faculty can also
request 10 hours per week of TA support. Rejection of TA support will not lead to an
increase in course equivalency.
3. A 0.75-Course equivalency credit will be provided in the workload for 3-credit courses
with enrollments of 75 -99 at the completion of the Add/Drop period. Faculty can also
request 10 hours per week of TA support. Rejection of TA support will not lead to an
increase in course equivalency.
4. A 1-Course equivalency credit will be provided in the workload for 3-credit courses
with enrollments of 100-150 at the completion of the Add/Drop period. Faculty can also
request 20 hours per week of TA support. Rejection of TA support will not lead to an
increase in course equivalency.
5. A 1.5-Course equivalency credit will be provided in the workload for 3-credit courses
with enrollments of 151-200 at the completion of the Add/Drop period. Faculty can also
request 30 hours per week of TA support. Rejection of TA support will not lead to [sic]
increase in course equivalency.
56

6. A 2-Course equivalency credit will be provided in the workload for 3-credit courses
with enrollments at 201-299 at the completion of the Add/Drop period. Faculty can also
request 30 hours per week of TA support. Rejection of TA support will not lead to an
increase in course equivalency.
Grievance Exhibit 2, College of Education and Social Services (CESS) Course
Equivalencies Guidelines, Revised March 9, 2022.
Faculty contributed to the development and editing of the Guidelines. “Faculty in all
Departments provided input into the document’s revisions via written comments and discussions
held during formal and informal meetings held in October and November of 2021, and
January/February 2022.” Id. at Notes.
The risk of harm the Union has identified in its Grievance, the loss of financial
predictability to faculty, was known to faculty when it participated in the development of the
Guidelines, and when they were published in March 2022. The Guidelines outline the change in
course equivalency credits that will be determined “at the completion of the Add/Drop period.”
Exhibit 2. The Union has not identified a new harm that could only be discovered by the passage
of time, nor has it outlined why it was unable to reasonably be aware of this harm back in 2022.
The Union has asserted the same harm or injury that existed back on March 22, 2022.
“Reducing a faculty member’s FTE after the add/drop period has the potential to seriously
impact the financial and benefit status of the faculty member and their family members.”
Grievance Statement at 5.
Faculty were aware, or reasonably should have been aware, of the existence of the risk of
harm which they assert in the Grievance when the Guidelines were issued in March 2022. The
publication of the Guidelines on March 22, 2022, disclosed the potential or risk that course
equivalencies could change and be impacted by the actual enrollments determined at the
57

completion of the Add/Drop period. The time to file the Grievance was back in 2022, within
thirty days of when the Union or Faculty or both were made aware or reasonably should have
been aware of this situation.
Grievant did not file its initial Grievance within thirty (30) days as required under the
CBA. The Board will apply the terms to which the parties have agreed and will not alter the
deadline.
The Board does not need to decide whether the Union has alleged an actual injury in fact,
because the Board has concluded the Union failed to file a timely Grievance with the University
by filing its Grievance of the Guidelines, issued by the Provost in March 2022, on October 8,
2024, well beyond the requisite thirty (30) days required by the CBA.
58

ORDER
For the reasons stated above, the motion to dismiss filed by the University is GRANTED.
Dated this 15th day of July 2025, at Montpelier, Vermont.

title: 38-60_Vermont State Employees' Association v. Vermont State Colleges
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
VERMONT STATE EMPLOYEES’
ASSOCIATION (VSEA) Docket No. 24-21,
v.
VERMONT STATE COLLEGES
VERMONT STATE COLLEGES FACULTY
FEDERATION
(VSCFF), AFT LOCAL 3180, AFL-CIO; Docket No. 24-27,
v.
VERMONT STATE COLLEGES
VERMONT STATE COLLEGES UNITED
PROFESSIONALS (VSCUP),
AFT VERMONT, LOCAL 6217, AFL-CIO Docket No. 24-35
FINDINGS OF FACT, OPINION, AND ORDER
Introduction
The Vermont State Employees’ Association, the Vermont State Colleges United
Professionals and the Vermont Colleges Faculty Federation (collectively “Unions”), representing
a total of seven bargaining units of the employees of the Vermont State Colleges (“Employer”),
each filed unfair labor practice charges alleging Vermont State Colleges violated the State
Employees Labor Relations Act when it unilaterally implemented a decision to deduct part of the
Child Care Contribution Tax (“CCC Tax”) from employees’ wages at the maximum amount
allowed by Act 76. The Unions challenge the imposition of the deduction as violative 3 V.S.A.
§961 (1) and (5).
60

The Employer disputes the charges, asserting that Act 76 imposed on it a mandate to pay
the CCC Tax and allowed it to take unilateral action regarding deductions from employee’s
wages. Because the imposition of the tax was a mandate, the tax was not the subject of
bargaining.
The parties provided stipulated facts and presented briefs to the Board Panel comprised
of David Boulanger, Acting Chair, Alan Willard, and Michelle Phelps.
STIPULATION OF FACTS
1. Vermont State Colleges (Colleges) d/b/a Vermont State University (VTSU) is an
employer under the State Employees Labor Relations Act (SELRA), 3 V.S.A. § 901, et
seq.
2. The Vermont State Colleges United Professionals (VSCUP), AFT Vermont, Local 6217,
AFL-CIO is the exclusive bargaining agent for a Professional, Administrative and
Technical (PAT) Unit (VLRB Docket No. 01-47) and a Supervisory Unit (VLRB Docket
No. 01-46). The former includes all full-time and regular part-time professional,
administrative and technical employees at the VTSU campuses, and the latter includes all
full-time and regular part-time supervisory employees at the campuses. At the time the
ULP was filed, the CBA had expired. On Monday, December 16, the successor CBA was
ratified, effective July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2028.1
3. The Vermont State Colleges Faculty Federation (VSCFF), AFT Local 3180, AFL-CIO,
is the exclusive bargaining representative of four units of employees: a) full-time faculty
1 The parties agree that the VLRB may take administrative notice of the CBAs and they may be referred to by the
parties or the VLRB in the briefs and decision.
61

and ranked librarians of VTSU (Docket No. 86-22); b) certain part-time or adjunct
faculty of VTSU, (Docket No. 91-01); c) certain part-time faculty of the Community
College of Vermont (CCV) (Docket 17-29); and d) certain part-time faculty of Northern
Vermont University Online (Docket No. 20-44). At the time the ULP was filed, the
applicable CBAs were set to expire August 31, 2024, except for CCV, which remains in
effect until August 31, 2025. On Monday, January 13, 2025, the successor CBA was
ratified for the full-time unit, effective September 1, 2024 through August 31, 2027.
4. The Vermont State Colleges Staff Federation, Vermont State Employees Association
(VSEA) is the exclusive bargaining representative all full-time, part-time, and limited
status non-faculty, non-professional and non-supervisory employees of the Vermont State
Colleges. (Docket No. 93-52). At the time the ULP was filed, the CBA expired June 30,
2024.
5. The VSCUP, VSCFF and VSEA are employee organizations under SELRA.
6. On or about June 20, 2023, Act 76 of 2023 became law in Vermont. The Act, now
codified at 32 V.S.A. §10553, requires covered employers to contribute the equivalent of
0.44 percent of each employee’s covered wages. This amount is known as Child Care
Contribution Payroll Tax. The Act further provides: “An employer may deduct and
withhold from an employee’s covered wages an amount equal to not more than one
quarter of the contribution required pursuant to subsection (b) of this section.” 32 V.S.A.
§10553(a)(1).
7. On July 1, 2024, Chief Financial and Operating Officer Sharron R. Scott notified all
Vermont-based VSC employees via email as follows:
Dear Vermont-based VSC employees,
62

In 2023, Act 76 (H.217), relating to child care and early education for
Vermonters, was passed into law. It created a Child Care Contribution (CCC)
under 32 V.S.A. Chapter 246, beginning July 1, 2024, where Vermont employers
and employees make contributions into the Child Care Contribution (CCC)
Special Fund.
The VSC recognizes the benefit of subsidizing child care for Vermonters,
including Vermont families, businesses, and communities. Effective July 1, 2024,
a 0.11% CCC Special Fund tax will be deducted from Vermont-based employees’
pay; VSC will pay the remaining 0.33% tax. The employee portion of the tax
equates to $1.10 for every $1,000 earned. For example, an employee earning
$45,000 annually will contribute $49.50 for the year; the VSC’s contribution for
this same employee will be $148.50.
For more information about Act 76 of 2023, including how it benefits you, your
family, and your community, please review the Vermont Department for Children
and Families Child Development Division’s FAQs at ACT-76-FAQs.pdf
(vermont.gov). The Let’s Grow Kids organization’s web site provides succinct
descriptions of Act 76 and its benefits: Vermont's Historic Child Care Bill —
Let's Grow Kids (letsgrowkids.org).
Our Payroll department is working with UKG, our payroll system vendor, to
implement the new tax. You will see the CCC deduction from all wages paid as
part of the first payroll in July. Should you have technical questions about how to
access your paystub, please email humanresources@vsc.edu.
Sincerely,
Sharron Scott
Sharron R. Scott
Chief Financial and Operating Officer
Vermont State Colleges
A copy of the Email is attached as Exhibit 1.
8. The Employer did not provide notice or opportunity to bargain to any union prior to such
communication or implementation.
9. As of July 1, 2024, all CBAs, except for the part-time faculty unit, the NVU online unit,
and the CCV unit, were subject to active successor contract negotiations.
63

10. The VSCUP collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) expired June 30, 2024, the VSCFF
CBAs were set to expire August 31, 2024 (except for CCV unit, which expires August
31, 2025), and the VSEA CBA expired June 30, 2024.
11. The Employer did not propose during successor contract negotiations to deduct or
withhold ¼ of the child care tax from payroll of any employee. On May 24, 2024, the
VSCFF had proposed (in bargaining for the full-time unit) that the Employer cover the
full child care tax. The VSCFF also proposed it again on June 20, 2024. On July 1, the
Employer notified the VSCFF that the implementation did not prevent the parties from
continuing to consider the VSCFF’s proposal in present bargaining.
12. The VSCUP did not make proposals regarding the child care tax, nor did it communicate
with the Employer regarding implementation.
13. On July 2, 2024, the VSEA sent a demand that the Employer cease and desist all such
deductions from employee payroll, and to communicate its intention to comply with the
law to bargaining unit employees. A copy of the email is attached as Exhibit 2.2
14. On July 3, 2024, the Employer denied the VSEA’s request and continued the deductions,
indicating that, if the VSEA desired, the parties should enter impact-bargaining A copy
of the response is attached as Exhibit 3. The VSEA declined this offer via email. A copy
of the reply email is attached as Exhibit 4.
15. That same day, the VSEA filed the instant unfair labor practice charge, #24-21, alleging
that the Employer unilaterally changed conditions of employment without providing
notice or opportunity to bargain. A copy of the charge is attached as exhibit 5.
2 The parties agree that the exhibits speak for themselves, and the stipulations merely summarize, rather than
supersede, the language contained within the exhibits.
64

16. On July 22, 2024, the VSCFF filed its unfair labor practice charge, VLRB #24-27,
asserting similar allegations as to its bargaining units. A copy of the charge is attached as
exhibit 6.
17. On July 22, 2024, the VSCUP filed its unfair labor practice charge, Docket #24-35,
asserting similar allegations as to its bargaining units. A copy of the charge is attached as
exhibit 7.
OPINION
The Unions assert the Employer violated the State Employees Labor Relations Act
(”SELRA”) by unilaterally implementing a decision to deduct part of the Child Care
Contribution Tax (“CCC” Tax) from employee wages and to deduct the maximum amount
allowed by Act 76 of 2023. The Unions argue the State was required to negotiate the amount to
be deducted from employee wages. The Employer claims that the CCC Tax under Act 76 was a
matter “prescribed and controlled by statute,” that did not impose on it a duty to negotiate the
amount to be deducted from employees’ paychecks.
The scope of issues subject to collective bargaining is broad under SELRA. See
Grievance of VSEA (re Prescription Drug Policy), 26 VLRB 305, 314 (2003). The statute
provides that “[a]ll matters relating to the relationship between the employer and employees shall
be the subject of collective bargaining except those matters which are prescribed or controlled by
statute. Such matters appropriate for collective bargaining to the extent they are not prescribed
or controlled by statute, . . . .” 3 V.S.A. § 904 (a). The Board construes narrowly exceptions to
the broad negotiation provision under SELRA, and the party asserting the exception bears the
burden of proving the exception applies. See Hackel et.al. v. VSC, 3 VLRB 175 186 (1980),
aff’d, 140 Vt. 446, 450 (1981).
65

The Employer argues that the CCC Tax under Act 76, was a matter “prescribed or
controlled by statute” and not the subject of collective bargaining under SELRA. The Employer
contends the “statute dictates how much the Colleges must contribute; the statute allows the
employer to share that burden with employees, and the statute limits how much the employer can
charge employees if it so chooses.” Employer’s Brief, at 8. The Employer also argues that even
if the Board were to find the statute does not prescribe or control the question of deductions for
employee child care contributions, the issue is not negotiable because the statute grants it the
right to charge employees a share of the tax at 0.11 percent of wages. The Employer asserts that
requiring it to negotiate this deduction strips it off this right granted by the Legislature.
Resolution of this matter requires review of the language of Act 47, to discern and give
effect to the Legislature’s intent. See IBEW Local 300 and Town of Roxbury, 30 VLRB 125,
132 (2009). Where the statute is clear and unambiguous, the Board must apply its plain and
ordinary meaning. See Grievance of Welch, 35 VLRB 19, 133 (2019).
Act 47 provides in pertinent part:
(a)(1) Each employer shall pay the Child Care Contribution on all covered wages
paid to each of the employer’s employees and shall remit those amounts to the
Department of Taxes pursuant to the provisions of this section. An employer may
deduct and withhold from an employee’s covered wages an amount equal to not
more than one quarter of the contribution required pursuant to subsection (b) of
this section. . . .
32 V.S.A. §10553
The first sentence imposes on Employer the mandatory obligation to pay the Child Care
Contribution on all covered wages. The Legislature chose the term “shall” when drafting the
first sentence, clearly expressing its intent to impose a mandate on employers to pay the CCC
Tax. The second sentence does not contain the same mandatory language. See New England
Phoenix Co., Inc. v. Grand Isle Veterinary Hosp., Inc., 2022 VT 10, ¶¶ 19-21, 216 Vt. 227, 234-
66

35 (2022) (comparing the Legislative choice of the word “shall” which the Supreme Court has
interpreted as imperative or a mandate with “may” which is permissive or discretionary).
Instead, having previously elected to impose a mandate in the first sentence, the Legislature,
chose instead to use the modal verb “may” in the second sentence, when outlining the
employer’s opportunity to deduct and withhold from employees’ wages a portion of the
contribution. Because the Legislature selected “may” in the second sentence to describe the
amounts to be deducted in contraposition to its use of the term “shall” to describe the CCC Tax
mandate, the legislative intent is clear, the deduction provision is permissive, not mandatory.
The second sentence also does not dictate the outcome of any negotiations on the subject
of employee deductions for child care contributions. The permissive language sets a cap or
ceiling on the amount of the deduction; it does not predetermine whether and what amount the
employer must deduct.
The Employer has not sustained its burden of demonstrating that Act 47 prescribes or
controls whether and what amount to deduct from employees’ wages for the child care
contribution.
The Employer has also not prevailed in its alternative argument that the child care
contribution deduction is not the subject of bargaining because the Legislature has expressly
granted this decision to the Employer. Responding to the Vermont State Colleges in similar
challenges, the Vermont Supreme Court has held that the legislative grant of authority to an
employer “does not preclude bargaining over all aspects of the power granted.” Hackel et.al v.
VSC, 140 Vt. 446, 450 ( 1981). That the Legislature has granted the Employer the right to
deduct and withhold amounts from employees to cover a portion of its CCC Tax does not render
the issue non-bargainable. See VSCFF, AFT Loc 3180, AFL-CIO v. Vermont State Colleges,
67

138 Vt. 451, 456-57 (1980) (holding that a statutory grant of authority to determine admission
and other educational standards does not render such subjects excepted from bargaining).
Nothing in Act 47 negates or undermines the express legislative intent that all matters relating to
the relationship between employers and employees are the subject of bargaining, except those
controlled or prescribed by statute. See3 V.S.A. §904(a).
The Vermont State Colleges engaged in an unfair labor practice by unilaterally deducting
one-fourth of the Child Care Contribution Tax from employees’ wages without providing notice
or an opportunity to bargain.
68

ORDER
Based on the foregoing findings of fact and for the foregoing reasons, it is hereby
ORDERED that Vermont State Colleges immediately cease and desist from deducting from
employees’ wages amounts for the Child Care Contribution Tax, reimburse or refund employees
for all such deductions, including an award of interest on deductions, and provide notice and an
opportunity to bargain.

title: 38-70_United Auto Workers, Local 2322 v. University of Vermont
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
UNITED AUTO WORKERS, )
LOCAL 2322 )
)
AND ) DOCKET NO. 23-43
)
THE UNIVERSITY OF VERMONT )
DECISION ON REMAND
On February 21, 2025, the Vermont Supreme Court reversed and remanded the February 20,
2024, Unit Determination Decision of the Vermont Labor Relations Board (“Board”) in which it
concluded that pre-doctoral fellows and trainees are employees for purposes of the State Employees
Labor Relations Act (SELRA), 3 V.S.A. §§ 901, 902. The University did not appeal, and the
Supreme Court did not review, the Board’s interpretation of the term “employee” under SELRA, nor
the Board’s specific factual findings and conclusions regarding graduate and research assistants,
other than to compare those findings with the lack of similar findings regarding pre-doctoral fellows
and trainees. The Supreme Court ruled that the Board decision lacked sufficient factual findings to
support the Board’s conclusion that pre-doctoral fellows and trainees are employees under SELRA.
The Supreme Court remanded the matter to the Board for further proceedings consistent with its
opinion.
On March 10, 2025, the Board Executive Director held a status conference with the parties to
determine whether they wished to file additional briefing on the issue remanded to the Board. The
parties agreed that they would provide targeted briefing on the issue. On April 10, 2025, the parties
filed with the Board final briefs and copies of the briefs they filed with the Vermont Supreme Court.
The Board has reviewed the transcripts, exhibits, and pleadings in this matter and issues its
remanded decision on the issue of the employee status of the pre-doctoral fellows and trainees. The
70

Board provides the following findings of fact, conclusions of law, and Order, and incorporates the
findings of fact from its February 20, 2024, decision.1
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. The University of Vermont (“University”) considers itself a research university and has been
striving to improve its ranking as a research university. Research universities are ranked
using the Carnegie classification, which classifies universities from very good research to no
research. At the time of the hearing, UVM was listed as an R-2, the middle ranking, with
hopes of moving up to an R-1 ranking.
2. The University benefits from the research conducted and the grants received by the
University, its faculty, and students.
3. The University receives about a quarter billion dollars or $250,000,000.00 in sponsored or
funded research grants. Of that amount approximately fifty percent is allotted to the
University towards sustaining its infrastructure.
4. The awarding organizations or agencies, like the National Institutes of Health, have
parameters for how the research funds will be spent. For the University to receive grants or
research funds, it must have personnel to perform the work of the research grant.
5. In recruiting Ph.D. students, the University competes with other universities nationally and
internationally. One of the tools it uses to distinguish itself and attract prospective students is
the overall financial support it offers students. The University makes its programs and the
1 The Supreme Court also identified confusion in the Board’s use of the term “assistantship(s)”
which the Board identified as referring to the entire group of approximately 627 graduate students
seeking membership in the proposed bargaining unit and the term “graduate assistantship” which the
Supreme Court interpreted as not applying to factual findings related to pre-doctoral fellows and
trainees. See Decision at n.1. To resolve any confusion, the Board will repeat findings that it
intended to also include pre-doctoral trainees and fellows.
71

accomplishments of its graduate students visible in the hopes of attracting graduate students
to the Graduate College.
6. A fellowship is a type of award or tool that the University uses to recruit the most
outstanding and diverse students. A fellowship is often awarded to bookend the Ph.D.
journey at the Graduate College.
7. The University offers two types of pre-doctoral fellowships depending on their source of
funding, either internal or external.
8. The source of funding for an internal fellowship is the University. A program, college, or the
University awards pre-doctoral fellowships directly to individual students on a merit and
competitive basis.
9. The source of funding for external fellowships are external or third party funding sources,
like the National Science Foundation or National Institutes of Health. With external funding
sources, the money flows through the University, which then distributes funds to the fellow.
10. Students are appointed as Predoctoral Trainees when their stipend is paid from a training
grant awarded to the University as opposed to the individual student. The University receives
the grant and pays the trainee from the grant.
11. Fellowships and traineeships may come with additional expectations, like mentoring and
networking. For example, the appointment letter awarded to Baxter Worthing includes the
requirement that they adhere to the requirements of the QuEST training grant. Union Exhibit
A.
12. Traineeships are designed to have additional expectations on the recipients that they
participate in specific experiences during their traineeship. For example, the appointment
letter awarded to Baxter Worthing includes the requirement that they adhere to the
72

requirements of the QuEST training grant. Union Exhibit A.
13. Fellowships may come with additional expectations, like mentoring and networking.
14. The amount of funds a student receives in a fellowship or traineeship (including stipend,
tuition scholarships and health insurance coverage) must be “at least equivalent to those
provided to GRAs and GTAs in the same program.” Employer Exhibit 13. Where the
program cannot provide equivalent funding, the program must figure out how to supplement
the funding to pay the fellow so that they are paid at least as much as the graduate or research
assistants.
Fellow and Trainees are employed by UVM
15. University publications and documents created to provide information to graduate
students, including pre-doctoral fellows and trainees, about their rights and
obligations refer to fellows and trainees as employees.
16. The Graduate College oversees pre-doctoral fellows and trainees. The UVM Guidelines
for Funded Graduate Students (“Guidelines”) govern graduate students in “work-based”
positions. The Guidelines apply to graduate students receiving funding as a “Graduate
Teaching Assistant, Graduate Assistant, Graduate Teaching/Research Assistant, or in a
Fellowship/Traineeship position.” Union Exhibit K.
17. The Guidelines establish an expected workload requirement to receive a full stipend.
18. The Guidelines provide that “[s]tudents receiving a full stipend devote, on average, .50
FTE effort (20 hours per week) to their teaching, research, or training duties during the
term of their appointment. The workload may vary.” Union Exhibit K. The Guidelines
also outline the holiday, sick leave, and time off policy.
73

19. The Graduate College determines the payment levels for stipends each year. Individual units
may alter the workload levels or stipend levels provided they are consistent with the
Guidelines.
20. According to the Guidelines, students funded by Assistantships, Fellowships or Traineeships
“may not work at UVM more than a total of .50 FTE or 20 hours per week” during the
academic year. Id.
21. The Guidelines also provide that students and their supervisors will provide notice to the
other about changes in duties, extra duties, and need for time off.
22. Fellows and trainees may lose their stipend or compensation if their performance is
inadequate or for gross negligence, dishonesty, or theft. Exhibit K.
23. The Guidelines outline the requirement for an annual appointment letter, setting forth the
term of appointment, salary, and any departmental conditions attached to the appointment.
24. The Graduate College reviews and approves appointment contracts between the
University and fellows and trainees.
25. The University sends an “Appointment Letter” to fellows and trainees outlining the
details of the positions offered through the Training Program or fellowship.
26. The details of the appointment letters are similar to those for research or graduate assistants.
27. The appointment letter outlines the length of the assignment, the stipend awarded, the
scholarship amounts awarded, health insurance coverage to be awarded, and the assigned
supervisor for the fellowship or training program.
28. The appointment letter provides that the fellowship and training grants are the only form of
“compensated effort” in which recipient students can engage without receiving permission
from the Graduate College.
74

29. Some appointment letters also detail when the first paycheck for academic year stipends will
be received. See Exhibit 17.
30. Fellows and trainees must complete an I-9 at the time of their initial appointment “to verify
they are either a U.S. Citizen or authorized to be employed in this country.” Exhibit 13.
31. The University advises graduate students that
Graduate students who are receiving any compensation for UVM employment
must, under immigration law, complete an Employment Eligibility Form known
as ‘I-9’before the end of their first day of employment.
Union Exhibit L.
32. The Graduate Student ePAR (electronic personnel action) contains instructions and
guidelines for completing the I-9 form. The instructions indicate that there are three sections
to the form, that “[n]ew employees and departments are responsible for sections 1 and 2.”
The system directs “employees” to fill out the first section. “Section 1 must be completed by
the employee no later than the first day of work.” Exhibit N.
33. In its Frequently Asked Questions for graduate students, the University explains when
payments or support to graduate students are taxable. The University recognizes support for
tuition and related expenses as not taxable because they do not represent compensation for
services. Exhibit L.
34. The University distinguishes non-compensable forms of support like tuition, from other
forms of support like living allowances, payments for travel or research, or internships which
“are potentially subject to income tax withholding and reporting.” Id.
35. The University also notifies its graduate students that “[c]compensation for teaching,
research, and/or other activities performed for the benefit of the University are also subject to
income tax withholding and reporting.” Exhibit L.
36. The University considers the pre-doctoral fellowship or training stipend to be taxable
75

income. Although it chooses not to withhold income taxes for the recipients and imposes this
obligation on the recipients.
37. Fellows and trainees are paid their stipend through the University payroll system, PeopleSoft.
38. Fellows and trainees, like other workers compensated for their services, must access the
“UVM Employee” pull down menu when accessing the PeopleSoft system. Union Exhibits
E, N.
39. The Biology Graduate Student Handbook for new graduate students, including fellows
and trainees, describes the following when answering the question about salary and
benefits:
First, review your contract letter, which contains important details
about your salary benefits as a graduate student. As a UVM
employee, your benefit and salary details are managed by the
PeopleSoft software package.
Union Exhibit Q (emphasis added).
40. Fellows and trainees are required to maintain a minimum GPA of 3.0 to continue to
participate in their fellowships or trainee programs.
41. The Graduate College resolves disputes regarding a failure to adhere to the terms and
requirements of a Fellowship or training grant. Exhibit 13.
Examples of Fellowship and Traineeships
42. Baxter Worthing (Plant Biology) and Bailey Kretzler (Plant and Soil Science) testified
about their experiences as fellows or trainees.
43. Baxter Worthing, a Ph.D. student in the Plant Biology Department of the College of Arts
and Sciences, has been enrolled continuously as a graduate student at UVM since the
76

fall 2018. He studies poplar trees and their ecological and economic benefits. Before
enrolling at UVM, Mr. Worthing obtained a master’s degree from Clark University in
2017. In the year between receiving his master’s and starting his Ph.D. studies at UVM,
Mr. Worthing worked as a lab technician for a biotech company in Boston.
44. During his first year, 2018-2019, Mr. Worthing was a pre-doctoral trainee through the
Quantitative and Evolutionary STEM Training (“QuEST”) program. As part of the
program, he was required to complete an internship outside of academia, participate in
training, and professional development seminars. The professional development
seminars involved providing feedback on the utility of professional development
seminars. To continue to receive the fellowship, he had to adhere to the specific
requirements of the QuEST program.
45. In 2020-2021, Mr. Worthing was a trainee under the QuEST program again because that
was the compensation vehicle offered to him. In this position, he worked on an applied
internship program at the Oakridge National Lab for the U.S. Department of Energy. He
received paychecks from UVM during the internship. He received a W-2 for the year he
was a QuEST trainee.
46. Bailey Kretzler, a Ph.D. student in the Department of Plant and Soil Science has been
enrolled continuously as a graduate student at UVM since 2020. She studies plant soil
microbe interactions in diversified agricultural systems, focusing on the plant soil
microbes in the three-system polyculture of corn, bean, and squash. She received her
Master of Science Degree at Lancaster University in the United Kingdom before starting
her doctoral program at UVM. She was admitted with three years of guaranteed funding.
77

She started her doctoral program in 2020 and during her first was a pre-doctoral trainee
through the National Science Foundation (“NSF”) QuEST program. The traineeship
provides a higher stipend level than the minimum stipend level for assistantships at
UVM.
47. As a trainee, she received tuition reimbursement and health insurance, like graduate
assistants. She was required to take training, complete an internship in a field outside
academia, interact with different disciplines, and participate in professional
development.
48. She was expected to work twenty hours a week on the traineeship. She had to adhere to
the specific requirements of the QuEST program to receive the funding. She was
supervised by her advisor and also program related faculty assisted in ensuring
compliance with the QuEST program.
49. In 2023-2024, Ms. Kretzler was “technically” a fellow. The compensation or funding
source was an internal fellowship with the Food Systems Research Center at UVM.
50. The work she performs as a fellow, and the supervision she receives, is the same as
when she was a research assistant.
51. Ms. Kretzler is compensated for her work as a fellow, which she accesses through the
PeopleSoft payment portal.
52. Ms. Kretzler is supervised in her work as a fellow. The entire time she has been at UVM,
including her time as a fellow, she has supported her advisor in the management of her
lab. She trains undergraduate students that come into the lab and facilitates lab meetings.
The lab management does not further her dissertation.
53. Ms. Kretzler uses the PeopleSoft program to facilitate her receipt of payment for her
78

fellowship. She used PeopleSoft as a graduate assistant and as a fellow. UVM paid her
through the program, and her payment was direct deposited. She received health
insurance through UVM but has to pay the premium.
54. The work performed through the fellowship or trainee is different from the aims and
goals of their academic programs.
55. Fellows and trainees are different from a scholarship or grant award because they
provide a service or benefit for the University. In exchange for this service or
benefit, the Fellows and trainees receive compensation in the form of a stipend.
56. The Fellows and Trainees perform the work assigned to them by a supervisor.
57. For the twenty hours of work or “effort” the fellows or trainees receive a stipend.
58. Fellows and trainees are regulated as employees under federal immigration laws, and
under federal and state tax laws.
MAJORITY OPINION
On remand, the Board reviews that portion of its decision in which it concluded that pre-
doctoral fellows and trainees are employees under the State Employees Labor Relations Act
(“SELRA”), 3 V.S.A. §§ 901, 902. Whether pre-doctoral fellows and trainees qualify or fit the
definition of employees under SELRA is relevant to whether they can be included in the proposed
employees seeking the right to self-organization and collective bargaining representation. See 3
V.S.A. §903(a). The Board, therefore, must determine whether pre-doctoral trainees and fellows are
employees under SELRA.
79

The applicable statute defines “employee” as a “State employee” that meets the definition of
section 902 (5), which provides as follows:
“State employee” means any individual employed on a permanent or
limited status basis by the state of Vermont, the Vermont State Colleges,
the University of Vermont, the State’s Attorneys’ offices, or as a full-time
deputy sheriff paid by the State pursuant to 24 V.S.A. § 290 (b), including
part-time employees, and an individual whose work has ceased as a
consequence of, or in connection with, any current labor dispute or
because of any unfair labor practice, but excluding and individual:
[subparagraphs (A) – (I) enumerated list of individuals excluded under the
statute]
. . . .
(J) determined after hearing by the Board, upon petition of any individual
desiring exclusion, of the employer, or of a collective bargaining unit, to
be in a position that is so inconsistent with the spirit and intent of the
chapter to warrant exclusion.
3 V.S.A. § 902 (5).
The statutory language is broad and defines employee to include “any individual
employed on a permanent or limited status basis” by the University of Vermont. Although
“employed” is not defined, the dictionary definition includes “to provide work to someone for pay.”
Heritage Dictionary (5thed. 2022). The United States Supreme Court, also referencing the dictionary,
provides the following definitions of “employee” in NLRB v. Town and Country, Electric, 516, U.S.
85 (1995):
The ordinary dictionary definition of employee includes “any person who works
for another in return for financial or other compensation.” Heritage Dictionary
604 (3d ed. 1992). See also Black’s Law Dictionary 525 (6th ed. 1990) (an
employee is a ‘person in the service of another under any contract of hire, express
or implied, oral or written, where the employer has the power or right to control
and direct the employee in the material details of how the work is to be
performed’).
80

The findings demonstrate that pre-doctoral fellows and trainees are under contract with the
University to perform services or effort on behalf of the University and the University has the power
or right to control them in material detail on how their work, service, or effort is performed. The
Graduate College monitors and issues an appointment letter to incoming pre-doctoral fellows and
trainees in which it lists the duration of service, the compensation to be awarded, the benefits to be
provided, the supervisor for the appointment, and the schedule for paychecks. The appointment
letter also limits and controls the labor of fellows and trainees by prohibiting them from engaging in
other “compensated effort at UVM.” Fellows and Trainees must sign the appointment letter to
indicate their acceptance of the appointment.
The University controls and limits the labor performed by the fellows and trainees. The
Graduate Guidelines detail the amount of labor or service fellows and trainees are expected to
perform to receive their stipend or compensation. The Guidelines prescribe that fellows and trainees
receiving full stipends, like other funded graduate students in “work based” positions, devote twenty
hours a week or .50 FTE effort to their duties. The Guidelines also outline the holiday, sick leave,
and time off policy. The Guidelines set out expectations that fellows and trainees will coordinate
with their supervisors about changes in duties, extra duties, and requests for time off. Fellows and
trainees can lose their stipends for insufficient work or for gross negligence or other forms of
misconduct.
Bailey Kretzler testified that with both her traineeship and fellowship she was required to
work twenty hours a week. Her supervisor directed and managed her work. The work she
performed as a fellow managing the lab and training undergraduates did not benefit her or her
dissertation.
81

The University admits through its own documents that fellows and trainees are
employees. The compensation the University provides to fellows and trainees is distributed
using the same payroll system as other UVM employees. “As a UVM employee, your benefit
and salary details are managed by the PeopleSoft Software package.” Union Exhibit Q.
Fellows and trainees, like other workers compensated for their services, must access the “UVM
Employee” drop down menu to access the payroll system and facilitate their payments. The
University materials explaining the I-9 form and process, use the term “employee” to describe
fellows and trainees who will receive compensation through payments from the University. In
its Frequently Asked Questions to Graduate Students, the University mandates that all
“[g]raduate students who are receiving any compensation for UVM employment must”
complete an I-9 “before the end of their first day of employment.” Exhibit L.
The University contends that fellows and trainees should not be considered employees
because, unlike graduate or research assistants, their funding source is portable which affords them
greater flexibility and discretion. This argument relies on a faulty premise and is otherwise not
persuasive. The traineeships and internal fellowships are funded through research funds awarded to
and distributed by the University. Indeed, the source of funding for Ms. Kretzler’s fellowship is the
Food Systems Research Center at UVM. The University controls the funding mechanism or source
of income for the trainees and internal fellows. The funds available through an external fellowship
are still administered by, or “flow through,” the University. The University monitors the fellows,
can remove them for inadequate performance, and applying the Graduate Guidelines expects from
them .50 FTE or twenty hours of effort each week. The University also benefits from the fellows
receiving external funds and working on projects and research that enhances the University and its
Carnegie classification.
82

The fellows and trainees are compensated for the service or work they perform for the benefit
of the University. The University receives 250 million dollars a year in research grants. One half of
that amount is retained by the University itself to sustain its infrastructure or operation of the
University and does not fund the research or students performing the research. Graduate students,
including fellows and trainees, supply the labor to perform the research required to receive and the
deliverables expected through these grants. The University benefits from the amount of funds it
acquires through research grants and at the time of the hearing it expected to attain the coveted R-1
Carnegie ranking because of this benefit.
The University distinguishes between financial support that primarily benefits the student
from financial support for service or effort that benefits the University. According to the
University’s own document, where the work or service performed by the graduate student benefits
the University, the compensation received for that effort is taxable. The University treats fellowship
and trainee compensation as taxable income. Fellows and trainees are compensated for the service,
work, or benefit provided to the University and their income is taxed.
The provisions of SELRA are sufficiently broad to include pre-doctoral fellows and trainees.
Fellows and trainees are employees as that term is used in SELRA. Fellows and trainees perform
service or work for the benefit of the University for which they are compensated. They are
“individuals” employed by the University of Vermont and fall within the jurisdiction of the Board.
The material similarities between fellows and trainees and teaching and graduate assistants
further supports that the former funded positions fit within the definition of “employee” under
SELRA. Any differences, like being denied a W-2, are not material or distinguishable when
evaluating employee status under SELRA. That the University imposes on fellows and trainees the
83

administrative burden of calculating their own withholding taxes does not disqualify them as
employees under SELRA.
Like research and teaching assistants, trainees and fellows cannot engage in additional
compensated effort at UVM without permission from the Graduate College. The Graduate College
oversees and administers appointment letters to both groups that outline the terms and conditions of
service, compensation, and benefits. The number of hours expected of fellows and trainees is
outlined in the Guidelines. Like graduate and research assistants, fellows and trainees must
complete an I-9 form before the “end of their first day of employment” to demonstrate they are
“authorized to be employed in this country.” Both groups can lose their compensation or positions
for poor performance or conduct. Both groups are directed by their supervisors in the performance
of their work or service. Fellows and trainees are compensated by and receive a paycheck from the
employee payroll system PeopleSoft.
As Ms. Kretzler testified, the work she performed and the supervision she received as a
fellow was the same as when she was a research assistant. Indeed, during her last year, her funding
source was a fellowship, but she performed the same role as she had the prior year as a research
assistant. Her supervisor was the same and directed her in her work.
Pre-doctoral fellows and trainees provide a service, work, effort, or benefit to the University
for which they are compensated or paid by the University and are supervised or monitored in
performance of such efforts.
84

The Board finds that the following is an appropriate bargaining unit:
All full-time and regular part-time graduate teaching assistants, graduate research
assistants, graduate assistants, and pre-doctoral trainees, pre-doctoral trainees/fellows,
and all other graduate students in other titles employed in an academic position.
Dated this 9th day of September 2025, at Montpelier, Vermont.
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
/s/ David Boulanger
David Boulanger, Acting Chair
/s/ Robert Greemore
Robert Greemore
85

DISSENTING OPINION
With all due respect, I disagree with the opinion of the majority on the application of the
exclusion provision of Section 902 (5) (J).
The positions in the proposed bargaining are so inconsistent with the spirit and intent of
the State Employees Labor Relations Act as to warrant exclusion. 902(5)(J). All of the positions
in the proposed bargaining unit are students and must remain as students to continue to receive
stipends and fellowships. The services the graduate assistants or fellows provide are in the
context of their role as students.
The relationship between the graduate assistants and UVM is primarily that of student-
teacher, with an educational rather than economic focus. The positions are fully integrated into
their academic programs. The rights and obligations that attach through SELRA are not
compatible with the overarching educational relationship between the University and students.

text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
RUTLAND NE PARAEDUCATOR )
AND BUS DRIVERS UNIT/ )
VERMONT-NEA )
